Apple’s Studio Display and Pro Display are seriously expensive, and they’re very much designed for professional and creative users who need 5K or 6K displays for graphics and video work. Not everyone needs such a high-res display though, and I’ve always found that a QHD (quad-HD) display with 2,560×1,440 resolution is the affordable sweet spot that works well for both general office work and off-duty entertainment. HP’s somewhat clumsily named E27u G4 is a good option here, providing an attractive QHD display with a variety of connectivity features for just $424/£286.80.
You’re not going to get a top-of-the-range display for that price, and the E27u does lack a few added extras, such as a built-in webcam or speakers. It gets all the basics right, though, with good image quality, multiple video inputs, and a useful built-in USB hub. The display’s 250 nits brightness may be relatively modest, but we found that the E27u looks bright and sharp enough for working with productivity software such as Microsoft Office, and also for streaming video from the BBC iPlayer and Apple TV+. And while Apple charges an extra £400 for an upgrade that allows you to adjust the height of its Studio Display—which is more than the entire cost of the E27u—you can tilt, swivel and adjust the height of the E27u, and even rotate it into upright (portrait) mode at no extra cost.
The E27u includes HDMI, DisplayPort and USB-C interfaces for connecting to your Mac, with the USB-C port also providing 65W power to charge a MacBook or other laptop if required. When using the USB-C connection you can also use four USB-A ports to connect devices such a keyboard, mouse or hard drive, and there’s also a second DisplayPort interface that will allow you to daisy-chain a second monitor if required. Our only complaint is that there’s no audio connector that would allow you to connect headphones or a set of external speakers to the display – although HP does sell a special ‘speaker bar’ that bolts onto the bottom of the screen if you want to add audio ($43.00/£40.00).–Cliff Joseph
How we test monitors
Macworld staff and other contributors with decades of combined experience have tested the displays in this round up. 
We thoroughly test each monitor, evaluating clarity of the image, maximum brightness, contrast ratio, and color accuracy and color gamut and other aspects of image quality. Motion clarity is also important, especially if the monitor will be used for gaming or other graphical applications.  
We also look at the build quality as well as usability and connectivity, and any special features or modes on offer, especially any that require software that may, or may not work as expected on a Mac. 
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld prides itself on our experience and expertise when it comes to all things Mac. We conduct in-depth reviews of numerous monitors annually. Our comprehensive recommendations undergo rigorous testing and evaluation by our expert reviewers, who adhere to both performance benchmarks and stringent usability standards.
Should I buy an Apple display for my Mac?
Apple sells displays for its Macs, and you could go with its offerings, which are included above, but its displays are a quite bit more expensive than what third parties offer. 
Buying from a different company may mean you may not get a feature that Apple offers, but it may also be a feature that you don’t need, depending on how you use the monitor. 
There are plenty of companies that have great monitors that you can use with your Mac, without having to take out a second mortgage. Our sister publication PCWorld has tested several displays, and we list their top-rated ones that we have been able to confirm work with Macs, alongside the monitors we have reviewed below. Here are our recommendations in order, starting with Apple’s most expensive.
Are there compatibility issues for Mac monitors?
There are compatibility issues for plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, which, unlike M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max/Ultra MacBooks, can’t natively connect to more than one external display. Fortunately, there is a solution and we show you how to connect multiple monitors to M1, M2 and M3 Macs in a separate article.
How to choose a Mac monitor
Display technology is a bit of a movable feast, with a lot of confusing jargon and technical features to wade through, as well as a variety of different interfaces and cables that are used by Apple itself and the various monitor manufacturers. So it’s worth taking a closer look at some of the factors that you need to think about when buying a monitor for your Mac.
Screen size
Size isn’t everything, as the saying goes, but it’s a good place to start. Your decision will be influenced by how much desk space you have, and how comfortable you are while using the display. Some people think that a big screen is best, but then when they start to use it daily, they find that it’s too big. And the same goes for customers who think a small screen is best.
If you’re looking for a size to start with for your own personal research, we recommend 24 inches—just like with Apple’s iMac. That seems like a good size for most people, and it’s easy to go up or down from that point. Most people tend to go between 24 and 27 inches for home use.
For professionals—graphics, video, audio, even spreadsheets—a large screen will help you be more productive. Think 27 inches and higher. You’ll be able to fit more elements on the screen and not waste your time scrolling.
If on-screen real estate is valuable to you, consider a multi-display setup. A smaller screen can be used for things like chat, email, web, and more, while the bigger screen is your main workspace. Or get screens of the same size and maximize the space.
Screen resolution
Screen resolution can go hand-in-hand with screen size. Screen resolution refers to the number of pixels used to create what you see on the screen. The higher the resolution, the more detail you can see. Larger displays tend to have more resolution options, as well as the ability to support higher resolutions.
Often, when you find two displays that are the same size but have a wide price difference, it’s mostly because of the screen resolution. Monitors with high resolutions are more expensive. For example, Apple’s $1,599 Studio Display is 27 inches, and it has a high screen resolution of 5120×2880 (5K resolution). On the other hand, LG sells the 27-inch 27UK650-W, but it’s a 3840×2160 (4K) resolution display for content creators, and it’s $350–lower resolution, but $1,249 cheaper. (There actually aren’t other 27-inch 5K monitors available, except for the $1,449 LG UltraFine 27MD5KL-B.)
So what screen resolution should you get? Here are some suggestions; these are guidelines that you can adjust based on your preferences.
For general purpose use, such as web browsing, email, media viewing, small photo and video projects and viewing: 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 (HD)
For more-involved content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 3840×2160 (4K)
For pro-level content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 4K or higher
Want to use an 8K monitor? Read How to connect an 8K display to your Mac.
Connecting a monitor to a Mac
How a monitor connects to a Mac can be confusing. The traditional HDMI and DisplayPort connectors used by many monitors are being replaced–or complemented–by USB-C and Thunderbolt ports. And though USB-C and Thunderbolt cables may look the same, there are actually some important technical differences between them, so it’s important to check which ports your new monitor uses and make sure you buy the correct cables and adapters.
Most recent Mac models have Thunderbolt ports, so if you buy a monitor that has HDMI or DisplayPort interfaces only, then you’ll need an adapter to connect to the Mac. This can get a bit confusing, but Apple does provide a list of the ports included on most recent Mac models so that you can figure out what you need.
Apple also provides a guide to HDMI and DisplayPort technology, which covers Mac models going right back to 2008, so that should provide all the info you need for all the Macs you use at home or at work. Less expensive monitors still tend to use HDMI and DisplayPort, and while it’s not too costly to buy adapters that will allow you to connect your Mac, we reckon it’s worth future-proofing your new monitor by getting one that includes at least one USB-C or Thunderbolt port.
If a display uses Thunderbolt to connect to the Mac, it may have additional USB-C or Thunderbolt ports so the display can act as a hub. In this case, If you have a device you want to connect to your Mac, you can connect it to one of the ports on the monitor, which is already connected to the Mac and probably in an easier location for access.  
Look for a USB-C or Thunderbolt connection with power delivery (PD) that can charge your MacBook. A 65W PD will be enough for a MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro, but you’ll need at least 90W for a 15-inch or 16-inch Pro.
Read our article on how to connect a second screen to a Mac which explains everything you need to know about how to identify which ports you have, the adapters you will require, and how to set things up.
Ergonomics
If you’re going to spend a lot of time sitting at a desk looking at your lovely new display then you need to keep ergonomics in mind. The ability to tilt the angle of the monitor back and forth, swivel it around for easy viewing, and adjust the height of the monitor in order to avoid an aching back or neck.
Some monitors can pivot or rotate in either landscape or portrait mode.
As a rough guide, there is a point at about 2 to 3 inches from the top of the screen that should be at eye level. Obviously, eye level varies from one person to another, so it’s important that you can adjust the screen for your own personal comfort. You may also prefer a monitor that doesn’t suffer from glare, or you will be forever repositioning the monitor (or your head) to compensate for that.
Other considerations
There are other considerations you’ll want to make when shopping for a monitor. A lot of these come down to personal preference or what you need for the work you do. They include:
Color space (gamut): The number of colors a monitor can show. Professionals need specific color spaces.
Refresh rate: The frequency when a screen is refreshed. Higher rates produce smoother animations.
Webcam: Some displays have a built-in camera you can use for FaceTime and other video conferencing apps, or to record yourself.
Speakers: If you plan on frequently viewing or listening to media, a good set of speakers makes for a better experience.
How many monitors does my Mac allow?
The number of external displays you can hook up to your Mac, depends on its M-series processor. In short, any Pro or Max M1 to M5 processor supports at least two monitors, but base M1/M2/M3 and Neo MacBooks might be limited to just one. See below for the full list and also a link to our tutorial about how to get round the limitations.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our DisplayLink workaround tutorial.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips in the link above.
• If your Mac has a base M4/M5, M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

content:

The Apple Support Community online shut down this past weekend. On this episode of the Macworld Pdocast, we’ll talk about why Apple did this, the repercussions, and what users can do. Tune in to the show! 
This is episode 1010 with Michael Simon, David Price, and Roman Loyola. 
Episode 1010 on YouTube






Episode 1010 on Apple Podcasts





Episode 1010 on Spotify






Get Info 
Click on the links below for more information on what was discussed on the show. 
Apple suddenly shutters its Support Community forums for no clear reason
Apple Battersea Store
First look inside Apple’s spectacular offices at Battersea Power Station (The Standard)
The story behind Toy Story (Disney) 
Comment Corner 
I thought the community was a good self- help part of Apple. A way to find out if others had similar issues, or if any workarounds or solutions were found. I would have thought even Apple people could get a feel for any trends in potential issues or feedback. Sure, there were people just ranting or expecting a direct connection with Apple. But the trend to just disconnect from users of your products just seems misguided.
John S. via email 





Isn’t it possible that closing the forum is an attempt to get people to try and use Apple Intelligence to fix their problems either so that it racks up usage and eventually they can charge people, or so the Apple LLM can build up its knowledge base and become the defacto AI source of information on Apple products and tech support for those products? 
 Jesse R. via email 





Since no new posts were allowed, I called the support number and I think I found out why they are closing the forums. They have instituted an AI system that walks you through solving your problem. It was very adaptive and the voice was pleasant. There were even background voices! Alas, it couldn’t solve my problem so I was connected to a real person. However, it seems that Apple is entrusting it’s support to AI rather than users. 
Gary B. via email 





I really hated to see this, as I have good memories of participating there often back in the early 2000s, when it really was more of a community. There were lots of really helpful and knowledgeable people, and often a real sense of camaraderie. 
As time went along, it did get less and less useful. I think a big part of it was Apple’s reorganization of the forum. It became hard to navigate to a particular area, like a section devoted to one particular Mac, one OS, one app, etc., where regulars who knew about that topic tended to hang out.  In addition to that, just the sheer growth of Apple and the massive amount of traffic, a lot from one-time users, made it really not possible to have the same kind of close-knit community anymore. 
And, admittedly, there are all kinds of alternatives now that are better options; but I guess I just have nostalgia for what it once was. I had a lot of good times and learned a lot there.

USB-C is the modern connection standard shared by most new devices today. It comes in several different formats—USB-C, USB4 and Thunderbolt—but they all have the same reversible connector at the end and are interchangeable and backwards compatible. All of Apple’s new devices now use USB-C or Thunderbolt for charging and data transfers.
Some cables are only really good for charging as their data-transfer (bandwidth) rate is too slow to be practical. In the reviews below we note both charging power (measured in watts) and data-transfer rate—measured in either megabits per second (Mbps) or gigabits per second (Gbps). If you are connecting the cable to a monitor, storage device, hub or docking station the minimum data speed should be 5Gbps but go higher if you can. If you just want to use it for charging an iPhone, iPad or MacBook, the data speed matters less.
We’ve tried and tested the best USB-C and Thunderbolt cables here. If you want to jump straight to our recommendations click the one that meets your requirements:
Best USB-C cable for iPhone and iPad
Best USB-C cable for Mac
Best Thunderbolt 5 cables
Best Thunderbolt 4 cables
You can find cheaper online but we recommend cables only from trusted brands, such as Anker, Apple, Beats, Belkin, Cable Matters, CalDigit, Native Union, Plugable, and Ugreen. When charging your precious devices, you want to be sure that you aren’t putting them at risk of overheating and potentially causing a fire in your home.
Apple’s old Lightning connector was also reversible—where it doesn’t matter which side of the connector faces up or down as you plug it in—so no big change there, but USB-C is much more than just a symmetrical design. It can transfer data much faster—pushing Lightning’s 0.48Gbps to up to 120Gbps, a 24,900% speed increase.
Apple’s iPhone 15 and newer have a USB-C port, replacing the old trusty but proprietary Lightning cable that has been a part of iPhones and older iPads since 2012. Apple supplies a USB-C charging cable in the box, but if you want a single cable for fast charging and data transfers—or just a spare charging cable—we’ve rounded up some of our favorites to help you get the best one.
Some are fast, some are super-powerful, some are both, a few are retractable, and some are just fun. Yes… fun!
We go into more detail about everything you need to know about USB-C cables after the chart of best cables, but for now you need to know about the cable of your dreams:
Which speed (measured in watts) your devices require: an iPhone needs at least 20W to fast-charge, an iPad 30W, a MacBook Air at least 70W, a MacBook Pro 100W and the 16-inch Pro 140W. While the MacBook Neo doesn’t officially support fast charging, a 30W charger will speed things up but any higher won’t likely do much more for that laptop model.
Do you need it to transfer data as well as supply power? Most charging cables are limited to a rather slow 480Mbps data rate. If you want proper bandwidth as well as charging power look for at least 5Gbps or as much as 80Gbps.
How long should it be: if the charger is within arms reach of your device a short cable might suffice where a long cable will just be an inconvenience, but if you want to charge your iPhone, Pad or MacBook while sat on the sofa a longer cable will make all the difference.
We’ve supplied the cable data to these questions in our reviews below.
The difference between USB-A, Lightning, USB-C, and Thunderbolt

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Thunderbolt looks identical to USB-C and uses the same connector, but is much faster. Thunderbolt 3 and 4 can reach 40Gbps, and Thunderbolt 5 stretches as far as 80Gbps (and even 120Gbps unidirectionally).
Note that the cables reviewed here are USB-C to USB-C (or backwards-compatible Thunderbolt to Thunderbolt). Old iPhone chargers had the non-reversible rectangular USB-A connector to connect to the charger and a Lightning connector that went into the iPhone. Don’t stick with legacy USB-A at one end as the old standard is limited in data transfer speed to 10Gbps and pegged back in charging speed to just a rather pathetic 15W.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Using a USB-C charger will enable fast charging even for iPhones with a Lightning port. You can still charge an Apple device with a USB-A charger but not at the fastest speed. From the iPhone 15 onwards it’s USB-C into the charger and USB-C into the iPhone. See our roundup of the best USB-C chargers for iPhone.
We have even more tips that show you the fastest ways to charge an iPhone.
Best USB-C cables for iPhone and iPad
Elsewhere we have rounded up the best Lightning cables we’ve seen for iPhones older than the iPhone 15. USB-A is the larger, non-reversible connector. USB-C is required for iPhone fast charging.
From the iPhone 15 onwards—also from the AirPods Pro 2—you’ll need a cable with USB-C on both ends (USB-C-to-USB-C) to charge an iPhone or iPad unless you charge wirelessly: check out the best MagSafe wireless iPhone chargers.
All iPads on sale today feature a USB-C connector. But even the 10th Gen iPad’s USB-C is still limited to a 480Mbps data speed. The iPad mini has a USB-C port that supports 5Gbps; the iPad Air 10Gbps; and the iPad Pro has a USB4/Thunderbolt port that can zip data along at 40Gbps. Check your iPad’s data transfer rate before choosing a new cable.
For charging only, any of the USB-C cables reviewed below will be fine as 20W should be enough to charge even an iPad. But if you are connecting to other devices or syncing via cable, we recommend cables that support faster data transfers. A 10Gbps USB-C cable, such as the Cable Matters cord below, is an excellent option if you don’t want to spend a bundle on Thunderbolt.

Thunderbolt  cables
Macs use the Thunderbolt standard that is faster and more capable than USB-C. If all you require the cable for is charging, then the relevant USB-C charging cable should be fine, but for anything requiring fast data transfers go for higher-bandwidth Thunderbolt. Thunderbolt cables are all certified to both speedy charging and very fast data-transfer speeds, whereas you need to check that the USB-C cables you think will do the job actually will—although buy from our recommendations above and you should be fine.
Standard copper “passive” Thunderbolt cables are also usually shorter as the data loses speed over longer distances. To get around this requires an “active” Thunderbolt cable that includes sophisticated chip engineering to push the signal along at the best speed, but you’ll see the price increase accordingly. Anything over 1m in length usually requires active technology.
Best Thunderbolt 5 cables
Thunderbolt 5 is superior to Thunderbolt 4 with doubled data/video bandwidth (80/120Gbps vs 40Gbps), improved PCIe 4.0 support (32Gbps vs 64Gbps), and enhanced power delivery (240W vs 100W). It’s backwards compatible all the way back to USB-C so—if you can afford it—it’s a more future-proof solution than Thunderbolt 3 or 4. Thunderbolt 5 transmits up to 80Gbps bidirectionally and 120Gbps in one direction with Bandwidth Boost enabled to support demanding display configurations.

Know your cables
Not all USB-C cables offer the same capabilities, so we explain each factor you need to consider. Fear not, for basic iPhone charging most USB-C cables will be fine. But some are finer than others. Macs use Thunderbolt cables that have the same Type-C connector as USB-C so look the same but have faster data transfer and charging speed options. You can use a Thunderbolt cable to charge USB-C devices, too.
Apple ships a USB-C Charge Cable with the newest iPhones but Mac users need to buy a Thunderbolt cable to connect to a docking station or fast storage device. Having a spare cable or two hanging around the house or office is always advisable—and there are better, cheaper, and more colorful USB-C and Thunderbolt cables than just those sold by Apple.
We’ve focused on USB-C charging cables as most people need them just to attach to a USB-C charger, but cables offer both charging and data transfers, although at different capabilities, depending on your requirements. 
Charging: All USB-C cables can carry a minimum of 60W (3A x 20V). Some support 100W (5A x 20V) charging, and some new Thunderbolt cables can charge at up to 240W. 60W is more than you need for a phone and is fine for the MacBook Neo and Air and 13-inch MacBook Pro. Go for at least a 100W cable for the 14-inch MacBook Pro. As Apple states 70W as the minimum for fast-charging the MacBook Air, a 100W cable is also recommended for these users. While 100W is fine for a 16-inch MacBook Pro, that model can be charged at up to 140W, although Apple restricts fast-charging for that model to its own $49/£49 USB-C to MagSafe 3 Cable, which is included with all MacBooks.
iPhone 15-16 series: Apple says that the iPhone 15-16 can be fast-charged from zero to 50% in 30 minutes using at least a 20W USB-C power adapter, which is the same speed the iPhone 14 got via Lightning. Tests have shown that such iPhones can reach charging speeds of up to 30W so we think a 20W charger isn’t going to offer iPhone charging as fast as you can get. 
iPhone 17 series: Up to 50% charge in 20 minutes with 40W adapter or higher paired with USB‑C charging cable, and up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with 30W adapter or higher paired with MagSafe Charger.
iPhone 18 series: Up to a 50% charge in around 15 minutes when using 60W‑capable adapter or higher with Adjustable Voltage Supply paired with USB‑C charging cable, and up to 50% charge in 30 minutes with 35W adapter or higher paired with MagSafe Charger.
Check out our reviews of the best iPhone chargers.
Length: A long cable can be messy when your device is close to the charger, but a short one could leave your iPhone dangling out of reach. You may need different lengths of USB-C cable for each of your charging spaces. When it comes to transferring data, choose a cable that’s as short as you need as the longer the cable, the greater the risk of signal degradation—invest in a Thunderbolt 4 or 5 cable for 2m data-strength confidence. Or look at a coiled cable such as the Native Union POP Cable reviewed above.
Data transfer speed: iPhones with Lightning ports are limited to a slow USB 2.0 data transfer rate of just 480Mbps (480 megabits per second). Compare that to your Mac, whose Thunderbolt connection can reach up to 40Gbps on Thunderbolt 4 and 120Gbps on Thunderbolt 5—that’s 250 times faster! Data transfer speed doesn’t matter if all you are doing is charging a device but it is vital when connecting your Apple device to storage drives, docking stations, or monitors.
While the entry-level iPad is also limited to 480Mbps, the iPad Pro, like a MacBook, supports Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps maximum. The iPhone 15/16/17 and 15/16 Plus features USB-C that is limited to 480Mbps as with Lightning, but the iPhone 15/16/17/18 Pro and Pro Max’s USB-C can sync at 10Gbps—useful for backing up video or photos to a computer.
Note that the USB-C cable Apple supplies with the iPhone 15-18 families is a “Charge” cable and limited to 480Mbps for syncing. If you use the Pro or Pro Max model with a cable for data transfer, you’ll do better with a 10Gbps or higher bandwidth cable.





 FAQ 


1.
Which USB-C cable do I need to connect to a USB-C monitor
DisplayPort Alternate Mode is a feature available to USB-C and Thunderbolt that handles video as if the USB-C cable was a DisplayPort cable. USB-C monitors can therefore connect directly to your laptop or via a USB-C hub or USB-C or Thunderbolt dock.
However, not every USB-C cable supports video transfer so you need to choose the right type of cable.
If your external display supports a direct USB-C connection, look for a cable that has at least a data-transfer rate of 5Gbps for 4K at 60Hz or 10Gbps for 6K. For 8K we recommend you use at least a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 or USB4 cable or 80/120Gbps Thunderbolt 5 cable. The higher the bandwidth, the less risk of signal degradation.
Consider cable length, too. While compression technologies should kick in, the longer your cable, the more the signal can degrade so opt for as short a cable as you require when connecting from your MacBook or dock to a USB-C monitor. A fully featured C-to-C cable that is 1 meter or shorter will work just fine for 95% of what people need. The Cable Matters 10Gbps/100W 1m USB-C Cable is a recommended solution.
If you need a longer cable, a 2m Thunderbolt 4 or 5 cable, such as the Cable Matters 2m Thunderbolt 4 cable. See the reviews above for more options.
Some USB-C monitors can provide between 65W to 90W of passthrough power back to the laptop, so ensure your USB-C cable supports at least 100W if you want to use your USB-C monitor to power your laptop.





2.
Can you convert a Lightning cable to USB-C?
Apple has released a Lightning–to–USB-C adapter—confusingly named the Apple USB-C to Lightning Adapter ($29 at Apple’s U.S. store or £29 at Apple’s UK store) so you can convert an old Lightning cable into a USB-C cable for your new iPhone 15 or later, but, as you might expect from Apple, it’s way more expensive than just buying one of the new and superior USB-C cables we’ve reviewed above.





3.
What is the difference between Active and Passive Thunderbolt cables?
An “active” Thunderbolt cable contains built-in electronic chips that boost and repeat the data signal, allowing it to maintain stable, error-free full-speed (40Gbps) signals over longer distances compared to shorter “passive” cables that lack these chips.

title: 1Password Security Breach: What Was Accessed and What Wasn't
content:
Popular password management app 1Password today said it experienced a security breach earlier this month. 1Password says some customer names and email addresses were accessed, but no customer vault contents were compromised.


On November 19, 1Password saw indications that an employee's GitHub account had been breached and began investigating. The company says the breached GitHub account was used to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, with the code downloading some customer data. Here's a list of what the hacker was able to get:

 	
Names and email addresses customers use to sign into 1Password

 	
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

 	
Public keys

 	
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (1Password says this can't be used for account access)

 	
Tokens in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

 	
Other non-secret account data related to 1Password's internal architecture, like version numeric identifiers and file numeric identifiers

 	
1Password source code, which 1Password says does not include customer data or user secrets

 	
Access to 1Password's CI/CD system, which it says has infrastructure-related secrets for the service to work


According to 1Password, there is no impact to its services, availability, or product security. Customer vaults and the items in them were not accessed, nor were the keys that protect vaults. The hacker did not have access to account recovery keys or 1Password apps and browser extensions. 1Password vaults are encrypted and protected by keys on the user end, so content is not accessible to 1Password or anyone who hacks the 1Password servers.

The biggest risk comes from the token breach. Tokens can be used for account recovery, but they only work when paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to a user's email address. Codes have now been changed from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them more difficult to brute force.

The affected GitHub account has been disabled, and the attacker's token was revoked. Internal credentials that may have been exposed have been revoked. Internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have been "tightened," with new detection methods for similar attacks. The company found no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using the exposed account provisioning tokens, and it has hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its response.

1Password users who had a token accessed were notified, but it is unclear if 1Password has sent notices about the breach to all users. While the blog post is titled as "update on" a security incident, it does not seem that the breach was disclosed when 1Password first learned of it six days ago.

1Password will not contact users to ask for an account password or Secret Key, and the information should be entered only in the official 1Password app or official website. It recommends all users be cautious about phishing attempts like emails, texts, and calls that mention 1Password or account recovery.

title: 1Password has been hacked–passwords are safe, but admin data was accessed
content:
Macworld





1Password is one of the most popular password managers, and one we’ve frequently recommended here at Macworld. Unfortunately, it has just suffered a major security incident.
On November 19, a malicious attacker gained access to a 1Password employee’s corporate GitHub account. They used that to access the 1Password source code and get access to the company’s backend services, which holds the administrative data for customers.
That’s stuff like customer names and email addresses, as well as public keys (but not private keys), account creation and sign-in times, and the like.
The good news for 1Password customers is that the content of user “vaults” were not compromised. That includes passwords and the other info that 1Password stores (like most password managers these days, 1Password can store payment info, addresses, and other data you may wish to auto-fill in forms). 1Password relies on private keys to decrypt passwords and other vault info, which are all hashed and salted so that even if an attacker decrypted one record it couldn’t get access to others.
1Password does not store your account password nor your secret key, which is used to generate the private keys stored on your own devices and necessary to access your encrypted info. All of that stuff is still safe. 
In the wake of the incident, 1Password disabled the GitHub account and revoked its key, rotated or revoked all internal credentials, lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters, and brought in an external cybersecurity firm to audit their efforts.
The company makes the following recommendations to users:
Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
If you see something suspicious, email support@1password.com.

title: An OLED MacBook Air is coming in 2028. Will it glow?
content:
Macworld





Last year, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple has plans to update the MacBook Air with an OLED display in 2028. In his most recent Power On podcast, Gurman reiterated those plans, claiming that OLED will be part of a MacBook Air “overhaul” over the next 12 to 15 months.
The current MacBook Air design was introduced in 2022. While the design is soon-to-be five years old, it doesn’t feel dated and aligns with the other Pros without a touch display. But now that a new laptop design has been introduced with the PROLED XDR Display, Apple will quickly move to update its other laptop designs so they don’t lose momentum.
What would a MacBook Air “overhaul” look like? Even though the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t all that visually different from the mini-LED MacBook Pro that Apple still sells, it’s different enough to set it apart in the line. Besides the OLED display, it features thinner bezels and rounder corners that expand the usable space further toward the bottom of the display (and macOS does a really cool trick with those corners). It also has a Dynamic Island instead of a notch.
More importantly to the Air line, the PROLED laptop is slightly smaller and noticeably lighter. The 14-inch PROLED XDR MacBook Pro weighs 3 pounds, about a half-pound less than the non-touchscreen model and about a quarter-pound heavier than the 13-inch Air, which weighs 2.7 pounds. If Apple can get the 13-inch Air down to 2.25 pounds or so, it’ll make a dramatic difference.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s major new feature is a touchscreen tandem OLED, but I don’t expect the MacBook Air to get such a high-end screen. These are premium features that Apple will keep on its Pro laptop–a tandem OLED is a costly component to put into an Air. More likely is that the 2028 Air will not have a touchscreen, and it will have a single OLED panel similar to the one in the iPad mini.
So, a thinner, lighter, OLED MacBook Air with more usable screen space. Sounds pretty nice. But what about the glowing Apple logo? It would be cool to see it on the 2028 MacBook Air, but I’m not counting on it. I think Apple will keep it as a MacBook Pro feature to set it apart from the Air and MacBook Neo. But who knows, maybe Apple decided it’s part of the design language covering all its laptops. That would be a nice touch.

title: Apple has made an iPad that runs macOS, but we’ll probably never see it
content:
Macworld





The release of the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has given new life to an old question in the Apple community: Will Apple ever release macOS on the iPad? We may finally have an answer, and it’s probably not one people are going to like.
On the latest edition of the Power On podcast, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said in no uncertain terms, “At this point, I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon.” Gurman revealed that Apple actually has iPads running macOS within Apple Park, but not for the purpose of releasing macOS on iPad to the general public. It’s for developing Mac-like features for iPadOS such as multitasking, and rebuilding Mac apps like Final Cut Pro for iPad. However, he cautions, “There is no work being done to consumerize macOS on the iPad,” said Gurman.
He’s on the side of the people who aren’t happy with that decision, however. “There are logic for the iPad. So they’re re-building a lot of the Mac and bring it to the iPad piece by piece, versus bringing the whole operating system to the iPad, he said. “In my view, I think they should just launch a 15-, 16-inch iPad and just bring Mac OS to it and just rip the Band-Aid off.”
But Guman notes that there’s another reason for keeping the iPad on iPadOS that’s complicates things further. In the European Union, it’s “better” for Apple to have distinct operating systems for its hardware segments, due to regulations. Considering how Apple swapped out Lightning on the iPhone due to EU regulations, it seems very unlikely that macOS will be released for the iPad.
Gurman does offer one glimmer of hope. Apple has been rumored to be working on a super-sized foldable iPad, something and opens up to a 19- or 20-inch display. Gurman said “it’s been facing a lot of issues” and was originally scheduled for 2027, but it’s been pushed out to 2029, if Apple decided to release it at all. Gurman said Apple is still undecided as to what operating system it will run. It could run macOS, iPadOS, or “something entirely new.”
creator: Macworld

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max Battery Exhausts a Toy Cyclops in New Apple Ad
content:
Apple today shared a fun ad highlighting the iPhone 18 Pro Max's battery, which offers the longest battery life ever in an iPhone.



In the spot, a cyclops toy comes to life and becomes enamored with the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max. The toy takes photos, plays games, uses apps, listens to music, captures videos, makes calls, watches TV, and uses the flashlight for shadow puppets.

The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max lasts through all of it, remaining at half charge when the cyclops's battery dies and the toy falls asleep.

Apple's ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max lasts up to 30 hours in "typical use," which is based on median iPhone usage. The metric includes messages, photo taking, music, social app use, streaming, games, browsing, and navigation.

Portable power banks that charge your phone are popular, but wireless battery packs using Apple’s magnetic MagSafe technology offer a simpler and smarter cable-free solution for iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and Air users. Special models that fit the iPhone Duo have also started appearing, and we’re testing them as they arrive at the Macworld Lab.
Phone batteries are prone to run dry just when you’re heading away from a power source, so having a portable charging source is one of today’s necessities. Annoyingly, most power banks require you to carry around a cable, too. Wireless power banks do away with cables but come with their own major limitation—the inefficiency of wireless charging means you need a high-capacity power bank to fully charge a drained iPhone.
MagSafe is a technology that’s compatible with all iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, Air and Duo models, from the mini to the Pro Max, but strangely missing from the 16e model. It allows accessories to clamp magnetically to the back of the iPhone, making the charging connection more efficient. Most standard magnetic power banks will connect with the iPhone Duo but are too long to maintain a firm grip when handled or placed in a pocket or bag—look for power banks designed specially for that model..
We put the best portable chargers through a series of rigorous iPhone recharging tests, and have listed the winners by power, portability and functionality:
Best high-capacity 10k MagSafe power banks
Best small portable 5K magnetic power banks
Best multi-device charging MagSafe power banks 
Best power banks for iPhone Duo
Best capacity magnetic power bank for you
You should consider size when it comes to a power bank: physical size and battery capacity. The higher the battery capacity, the more recharging power you’ll get from the power bank—but you’ll also be carrying around a larger, heavier item. Lighter, slimmer power banks are easier to pocket even when clamped to your phone. Larger power banks might not fit in your trouser pocket and can slide off easier when pocketed even if clamped magnetically.
10K power banks (with a 10000mAh battery capacity) can charge a phone close to two times over, while 5K (5000mAh) battery packs usually stretch between 60-75%, which is often enough to get you to the next wall-socket powering opportunity. If you are relying on the power bank for long-haul travel or a camping trip, a 10K battery or higher will suit you better. Belkin even offers a mid-range 8K power bank.
Milliamp hours (mAh) is quite a blunt measurement of battery capacity. It’s great for quickly differentiating between power bank sizes but we also list the capacity in the more accurate watt hours (Wh).
Also, look out for power banks that are built using the latest semi-solid-state battery technology that uses less liquid electrolyte than standard litium-ion power banks, making them more durable, longer lasting, and safer.
Wireless power bank charging speed
Wireless charging speeds vary from 7.5W (MagSafe Compatible) to 15W (certified MagSafe and Qi2), all the way to the very fastest wireless charging at 25W (Qi2.2). While it’s not as efficient as using a cable to charge a phone, magnetic wireless charging is a step closer to doing away with cables altogether. Qi2 25W brings wireless charging close to wired speed but only iPhones 16 and later support that speed, and some power banks include a built-in USB-C cable for even faster charging up to 45W. The iPhone Air can manage 20W max on even a 25W charger. See Which wireless tech is best for your iPhone?.
We have listed the speeds at which each portable power bank can be charged itself (Input charger) and charge the iPhone (Output charger). The higher the wattage, the faster the charging should be.
Best high-capacity 10K MagSafe power banks
A 10000mAh (10K) battery is the sweet spot for both power and portability. 5000mAh (5K) power banks reviewed further down are slimmer, lighter and easier to pocket, but generally offer a maximum of 70-80% recharge potential versus a 10K power bank that should be able to recharge an iPhone at least one and a half times over.

The Kuxiu S3 was the first semi-solid-state 25W magnetic wireless power bank to enter the Macworld Lab. A semi-solid state (SSS) power bank is more energy-dense than a traditional liquid electrolyte power bank because its semi-solid electrolyte is less prone to leakage and thermal runaway. SSS is therefore more durable, safer and offers more charge cycles so will last longer.
Indeed, not only does it tick those boxes but its also boasts three other top-end features: a built-in USB-C cable, integrated kickstand, and super-clear digital battery display.
Only the iPhones 16/17/18 support the very fastest wireless tech Qi2 25W, and only the iPhone 15 and later have a USB-C charging port. Older iPhones (from 12 on) can use a 25W charger such as the S3 but are pegged back at 15W—still faster than the 7.5W found on cheaper power banks.
Switch to wired charging via the integrated USB-C cable and you’ll achieve up to 35W so even faster.
The S3 has a 10000mAh (10K) battery capacity and managed to recharge that same iPhone to 177%—so up to 100% then another 77% when it came to a second recharging task. That’s not the top score we’ve had in our 10K power bank tests: the champ so far is the Ugreen MagFlow Air 10K, which scored an unmatched 208%, with the EcoFlow RAPID 10K and Anker MagGo Slim scoring 190% or close—both are reviewed here. But 177% is above average.
The same company offers two other 25W magnetic power banks: the similar S4 reviewed below, and the K1 Ultra (reviewed in our multi-device section below) that has a neat slide-out panel that can charge your Apple Watch or AirPods at the same time as the iPhone.

The Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro has two charging modes, which you activate with the charging button while looking at the display. Silent Mode is without the fan on, and Cool Mode is with the fan working for slightly faster charging.
You can tap through six screens on its large, informative digital display to check charging status, battery level, battery health, and temperature, or quickly switch Silent and Cool charging modes and wireless charging on or off.

The EcoFlow RAPID 10K has a large capacity, refilling a iPhone 16 Pro twice over in our tests—close to the best we’d seen, with only the Ugreen MagFLow Air 10K beating it. What makes this power bank special—although not unique—is its short built-in USB-C cable that can be used for fast-charging an iPhone 15, 16 or 17 or refilling the power bank itself. The cable fits neatly away when not in use at the bottom of the power bank. It’s the highest rated we’ve tested with 65W input and output. 
Wirelessly it will work with any MagSafe iPhone (12/13/14/15/16/17/18) at 15W. iPhone 15/16/17/18 users can connect via the integrated USB-C cable or a separate longer cable via the side USB-C port if required, for faster 30W charging. Owners of earlier iPhones can use a USB-C to Lightning cable instead for fast 20W wired charging from the power bank’s port. Note that the iPhone 16e does not work with magnetic wireless charging.
For faster wireless charging, consider the new generation of Qi2 25W power banks such as the Kuxiu S3, Baseus PicoGo and Iniu SnapGo Air reviewed here. That said, the 25W power banks we have tested didn’t match the EcoFlow or Ugreen MagFlow Air on battery capacity in our tests, although they are not too far behind.
No 10K magnetic wireless power bank can match the EcoFlow on input speed—that is the rate at which it is recharged itself. Its 65W is much faster than the average 30W input speed.
While winning on charging performance and capacity, the EcoFlow Rapid is reasonably chunky compared to the Ugreen MagFlow Air, Anker MagGo Slim and Benks ArmorGo, and notably bulkier than smaller-capacity 5K power banks. It’s still pocketable but the slightly larger size is the compromise for the other benefits. If you want a slimmer battery pack, look for a smaller 5000mAh option—we’ve tested the best slim power banks further on. It has a handy pull-out kickstand at the back.

This 25W wireless power bank lived up to its claims of wirelessly charging an iPhone 16 Pro from 0% to 50% in 36 minutes—12 to 15 minutes faster than a 15W power bank. That might not sound a lot but when you’re in a rush to charge your phone, every minute counts. 25W wireless charging is limited to the iPhone 16 to 18 families, running at least iOS 26; older iPhones will charge at 15W using this power bank.
Most 10K wireless power banks are around 22mm deep, so the 16mm-thin Baseus PicoGo Magnetic 10K Power Bank (AM52) is one of the slimmest we’ve tested. The Kuxiu S4 reviewed above is even slimmer at just under 14mm but the AM52 is certainly thinner than most.
The AM52 is an output blazer is more ways than one. It is certified Qi 2.2 so charges wirelessly at 25W, as fast as the Ugreen MagFlow reviewed below, and like the MagFlow also boasts an option with a built-in USB-C cable. And if you choose wired charging, you can access output at 45W—equal fastest of any magnetic wireless power bank reviewed with the Iniu SnapGo Air, Ugreen MagFlow Pro and Anker MagGo 2 reviewed above. If you use the wireless charging pad, the handy integrated USB-C cable and the spare USB-C port to simultaneously charge three devices—say your iPhone, Apple Watch and AirPods—total output is restricted to 15W.
When recharging an iPhone, it refilled our test 16 Pro more than one and a half times, scoring an impressive 182% in the Macworld Recharge Score. 
The Baseus PicoGo AM52 costs $69.99 / £59.99 for the model with no integrated cable and $79.99 / £69.99 for the AM52 with cable built in. We think that extra ten bucks is worth it for the convenience of the built-in cable. Both are also available in Apple’s new Burgundy color (here called Dark Cherry).

If you really want a violet power bank, the Lisen P604 is ready for you, as well as being available in a rather fetching Sandstone hue, plus the usual black and white. The P604 is a curious 10K power bank in a couple of other ways, too.
In the U.S. it claims to have a USB-C power output of 65W, which would put it right at the top of the charts in terms of wired charging, as well as it boasting Qi2.2’s 25W wireless charging. However, because that’s a  “burst speed” that can’t be maintained throughout the charge, in some other nit-picking regions (e.g. the U.K. and E.U.) it is listed as a 45W wired charger. 45W is still extremely fast for an iPhone, but don’t be surprised to sometimes see it listed as either 65W or 45W or both, which is a little confusing. As a result, we’ll regard it as 45W here, but you might get an initially faster charging experience with this power bank tahn with others when using a cable.
The other variance to other power banks is its slightly humped back in comparison to the flat form of most portable chargers. It means it’s a little shorter but thicker than most.

If you want to get the 60W charging use either the USB-C port or cable and have nothing else hooked up to the power bank. 
It features built-in U.S. plug prongs so can be connected straight into a power socket rather than requiring a separate USB-C charger. You can quickly charge the power bank plugged into a wall AC socket, but during recharging the output is reduced to 20W on the port and cable until the battery is at 100% when the charging returns to 60W. The U.S. plugs are fine for users based in North America, but not for international users, so there are U.K., E.U, and AU/NZ plug adapters included making it work in those countries and as a travel companion.

How we tested
MagSafe charger testing was conducted using an iPhone 16, 17 or 18 Pro, subscribed to a 5G network and WiFi, with screen off and all default settings.
Our test is a simple battery recharge shootout. We let our test-unit iPhone Pro (3095mAh battery capacity) drain to just 10% and then set the Battery Pack to work recharging the phone. We then assigned the charger a score of whatever percentage it managed to charge the iPhone to and subtract the 10%; we test each model at least twice.
It’s not a real-world test of day-to-day use where you’ll likely be using your phone for various tasks (of varying battery usage) and in different environmental conditions and network configurations. But it does give us a common score format that we can use to compare different battery-pack models.

				
					

				
			
Why is magnetic wireless better?
The MagSafe connection to Apple’s iPhone is precise enough to make wireless charging more efficient as around 20% of non-magnetic power loss is from poor placement of a phone and the wireless charging pad. Standard Qi wireless charging can lose as much as 50% of the portable battery’s power, but MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging loses ‘just’ 30%. Hot out of the gadget laboratory, the new Qi 2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) brings even faster 25W wireless charging for the iPhone 16, 17 and 18. 15% will be plenty fast enough for most of us but who doesn’t want the fastest possible charging when your iPhone’s battery icon is in the red?
Why comparing Watt Hours is better than Milliamp Hours
Phone batteries are generally rated in Milliamp Hours (mAh) but this is a measure of electrical charge, while a Watt Hour is equal to one watt of energy consumed for one hour of time.
When comparing battery capacities and how much a power pack will boost a phone’s internal battery, energy is more important than electrical charge.
And mAh ignores a battery voltage, which determines the wattage (power) of a battery.
If the mAh is the same, the higher the voltage, the greater the actual stored power.
For example, Apple’s MagSafe Battery Pack is rated at just 1460mAh but it has a higher voltage potential (7.62V) than the iPhone (3.81V) or other battery packs, meaning that it can provide more power to an iPhone than its mAh suggests; in fact, it is actually 2920mAh.
To go into further depth about this read our feature iPhone battery capacities compared that also lists all iPhones battery life in mAh and Wh.
Anatomy of a magnetic power bank

				
					

				
			
TORRAS




A lot more than a battery goes into the making of a magnetic power bank.
Of course, the battery is the most important component, but the wireless charging coils and magnetic connection are vital for efficient and therefore fast and powerful charging. The transmitter coil transfers power by electromagnetic induction.
The magnets need to be set up to exactly connect the transmitting coils—here on the power bank— to the receiving coils, in this case inside the iPhone.
The example shown above is the Torras MagStall Wireless Power Bank, reviewed in our chart. You can see the various parts, including that power bank’s rotating stand/handle.
Which magnetic wireless tech is right for each iPhone?
iPhone 7 and earlier: Don’t support wireless charging. 
iPhone 8 – iPhone X/XS/XR: Support wireless charging. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly at 7.5W but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 11 and earlier: Don’t support MagSafe. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 12 – iPhone 15: Support MagSafe and Qi2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, and at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers.
iPhone 16 – iPhone 18, plus iPhone Duo: Support MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2.2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers, and at 25W with Qi2.2-certified power banks and chargers.
Is charging via a cable faster or safer than magnetic wireless charging?
Charging via a cable is nearly always faster than wireless, even the latest Qi2.2 wireless chargers. Wireless charging is inefficient, losing some of its energy transfer through heat, for example. MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi2.2 magnetic connections dramatically improve efficiency but sticking a cable in is still a faster method, if not as convenient.
Most magnetic wireless power banks include at least one USB-C port, and some even include a port and an integrated cable for ultimate convenience. Models after the iPhone 17 can charge to 50% in 20 minutes or under via a cable and a 45W or higher charger or power bank. But wireless is so simple and cable-free that we don’t mind waiting an extra 15 minutes or so to reach such a charge wirelessly.
Why does my phone occasionally charge slowly or even stop charging?
This phone charging behavior is due to the built-in battery management feature on your iPhone. A phone heats up during charging as power is exchanged between the charger’s coils and the iPhone’s own. The phone actively adjust its charging behavior accordingly. This can slow down or temporarily pause charging to protect battery health and extend its lifespan. This is completely normal. Once the phone cools down, charging will automatically resume as normal.
What is a semi solid state battery?
The material that carries ions back and forth inside a battery is called “electrolyte”. Traditional lithium-ion batteries use a volatile, free-flowing liquid for electrolyte. As their name suggests, solid-state batteries use a solid material such as a ceramic or polymer. But semi-solid-state batteries are more common in today’s new generation of power banks.
A semi-solid-state battery uses a mix of solid particles in a much smaller amount of liquid, making a hybrid thick gel, paste or slurry. By reducing the liquid content to a minimum, semi-solid-state batteries increase stability and durability and significantly lower the risk of leaks, fires, and dangerous thermal runaway.
What about non-wireless power banks?
Wireless charging—especially magnetic wireless charging—is super convenient and does away with the need to carry around messy cables to connect your device to the battery pack.
But wired charging is nearly always faster and not much of an inconvenience if you are not out and about. Over on our sister site Tech Advisor I have reviewed the best power banks that includes standard non-wireless battery packs that might be a decent solution as well as the power banks reviewed above.
Do magnetic power banks work when the iPhone is in a case?
Yes, most quality iPhone cases are compatible with MagSafe having their own magnet ring to ensure a close connection between the power bank’s magnetic charging coils and the iPhone’s own. You can find exactly which are supported in our roundups of the best iPhone 18 cases, best iPhone 17 cases, and best iPhone 16 cases.

title: Apple Has an iPhone Notifications Problem
content:
Apple has rules in place that are supposed to protect iPhone users from unwanted advertising in push notifications and Live Activities, but some apps appear to be flouting these rules, and Apple does not appear to be consistently enforcing them.


Apple's App Store guidelines do allow iPhone apps to send push notifications for promotions or direct marketing purposes, but only if users have "explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed" in the app, and so long as the app provides a method "for a user to opt out from receiving such messages."

Push Notifications should not be used for promotions or direct marketing purposes unless customers have explicitly opted in to receive them via consent language displayed in your app's UI, and you provide a method in your app for a user to opt out from receiving such messages.
Unfortunately, there are some examples of apps ignoring this guideline.

On my iPhone in Canada, there are several apps that send me push notifications containing promotions without offering a way to opt out of these promotion-specific notifications, such as Cineplex, McDonald's, and Wendy's.

Canadian food delivery app Skip does offer a setting to turn off promotional notifications, but it has continued to send them to me long after I opted out.


Do you have any iOS apps that don't respect your promo notification settings or don't let you turn off promo notifications as Apple requires?

Let me know for a MacRumors story!

— Joe Rossignol (@rsgnl) November 25, 2026



A few MacRumors readers informed us that after they turned off DoorDash notifications for offers specifically and then place a delivery order, the app will prompt users to re-enable notifications so they "never miss an order update," even though they still have notifications enabled for order updates. The wording of this prompt can trick users into thinking that they might not receive order updates, but tapping the button re-enables offers.

app design guidelines saying "don't use a Live Activity to display ads or promotions" under "best practices." Apple's App Store guidelines say apps should not send users "unsolicited messages" via Live Activities.


Never expected to see anything like this https://t.co/GbdRIfqaE2
— Out of Galaxy (@OutofGalaxyy) November 22, 2026



If you know of other offending apps, let us know in the comments section. There are more.

Apple recently sent out its own App Store notification advertising a Paramount+ subscription deal, but the App Store does offer an option to opt out. Open the App Store, tap on your profile picture in the top-right corner, tap on Notifications, and turn off Recommendations & Offers. However, it is not clear if Apple obtained explicit consent from users as its App Store guidelines require. Of course, the App Store is a preinstalled app, so it technically does not have to follow the rules that Apple sets for third-party App Store apps.


PUSH ads now?! https://t.co/WRBndvxbE3
— Dylan (@DylanMcD8) November 21, 2026



All in all, it appears that Apple needs to do more to crack down on apps that are violating its rules surrounding advertising in push notifications and Live Activities.

title: Apple Is Far From Done With 2026: Here's What's Still Coming
content:
Apple's busiest season isn't over yet – far from it. With Black Friday kicking off this week, plus new products, software updates, and new smart home accessories running into December, there's more on the way from Apple before the end of 2026, so be sure to stick around.


Below, we've rounded up what's still coming, along with one date in particular that's worth watching if you're a holiday shopper.


Black Friday – November 27: Not a product launch unfortunately, but a date likely worth marking. Apple's annual four-day shopping event runs from Friday, November 27 through Monday, November 30, with gift cards worth up to $300 offered with eligible purchases. Apple is also offering new and qualified returning subscribers the Apple TV streaming service for $6.99 per month for six months, with that deal available until November 30. Our Black Friday roundup will be tracking all the deals.

(PRODUCT)RED AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 – expected December 1: Apple plans to release (PRODUCT)RED versions of the existing AirPods Max 2 and HomePod mini 2 on or around Tuesday, December 1, which is World AIDS Day, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The new color is expected to be the only change. Apple is also releasing a red Wrist Strap for AirPods Pro and a red Sport Band for the Apple Watch.

App Store Awards – expected December: Apple named this year's finalists on November 18, and the winners are expected in the coming weeks. Last year, Apple announced the winners on December 4, so a similar early-December date looks likely this year.

Apple Music Replay – expected December: The full 2026 Replay recap is likely to arrive around the same time as last year's, when the full version became available on December 2, with your top songs, artists, and listening stats for the year.

iOS 27.3 – December: Apple says iOS 27.3 will be released to the public in December, though it hasn't given a date. The first iOS 27.3 beta arrived on Tuesday, November 3. Beta features can change before release, but so far it includes new Siri AI actions across apps, vertical tabs and an Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, the redesigned Health app, a new Apple Fitness+ Gym Strength workout that builds a four-week plan, and more. Our iOS 27.3 beta guide has the full list.

Apple Intelligence in China – December: The first Apple Intelligence features for users in China are already in testing in the iOS 27.3 beta, and Apple has confirmed the public rollout for December alongside the update. Apple has partnered with Alibaba to add Qwen support to Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence. The initial release is for supported iPhones, with other platforms to follow after the required regulatory approvals, and it does not include Siri AI.

Apple Home Collection – from December: The new Apple-backed, third-party lineup includes smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple says that availability begins in December, although select accessories will not arrive until early 2027.

title: macOS Tahoe’s enormous window corner radii make so much sense now
content:
Macworld





Back when macOS 26 Tahoe was introduced, the corner radius was something of a controversy. For reasons unbeknownst to users, Apple opted to increase the roundness of the window corners, from 10-point on previous versions of macOS to 26-point in Tahoe.
The slight change was extremely noticeable. Windows looked amateurish, older apps didn’t match the new style, and even Apple was inconsistent within its own default apps. And what’s worse, windows were harder to resize when trying to grab them by the corner—it was a mess. To make matters worse, the windows didn’t even match the corners of the Mac’s screen. The 26-point radius was closer to the iPhone than a MacBook or iMac, and everyone just assumed the change was due to laziness or poor quality control.
In macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple changed back to a more sensible 20-point radius. People rejoiced and assumed Apple listened to the criticism, realized its mistake, and made the necessary adjustments.
But now I’m not so sure it was a mistake. I hadn’t realized this before, but the new rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii. And you can actually see it in action. Check out this gif:

				
					

				
			
Roman Loyola/Foundry




What’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.
So it seems like what we thought was a bit of lazy design was just a peek at what was to come from the MacBook. Back then there wasn’t a curve at the bottom of MacBook screens, so there was nothing to see yet, and the overly rounded corners were something of an experimentation for a machine that was still in development.
So remember, Apple may make mistakes, but it doesn’t usually do things by accident—even if we might not like the explanation.

title: Anthropic unveils Claude-powered easy button for making Mac apps
content:
Macworld





Anthropic announced Tuesday that it is rolling out beta access to a new feature in Claude for Macs that allows users to save “artifacts” as apps. When a user creates an artifact app, it appears like a native Mac app that opens in its own window, rather than in the Claude app, essentially operating as an independent app. Artifact apps have their own icons and can be shared with others like normal Mac apps.
Artifacts are projects that users create in Claude separately from the standard chat interface. Users can describe what they want their project to do, and Claude will create it. Users can adjust, edit, and tweak the design and functionality either manually or through conversations with Claude. They typically live inside a separate section in its sidebar for artifacts, and users typically use this space for creating things such as documents, graphics, code, and other projects. Artifacts are available on all Anthropic plans: Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans.
Artifact apps can use Claude and its connectors, and they automatically update whenever someone with permissions makes changes. Apps can send notifications or add items to the Mac menu bar or system tray. However, any requests the artifact app makes count towards your plan’s usage limits. Anthropic shared a list of apps created by people at the company:
Vitals, a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance
Linnet, a full layered image editor
Phosphor, a file manager that looks made for a movie set
Sift, which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized
Tern, a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain
The artifact app creation beta is rolling out on all Claude plans but is not available to HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments. The Claude app is required to launch an artifact app.
creator: Macworld

title: Claude Now Lets You Install Artifacts as Desktop Apps
content:
Anthropic has released a new feature for Claude that allows users to install artifacts as desktop apps on macOS and Windows.


Artifacts are documents, designs, dashboards, and interactive tools that Claude creates in a panel alongside your chat, where you can view and edit them.

When you ask Claude to create an artifact, you can now click "Install as app" in the Share menu, after which you'll be able to launch it in its own dedicated app window and see it in the Dock.

Artifact-based apps don't need to be packaged or signed, but they do need a permission level to be set. Choosing Default permissions means they can only do what they'd be able to do in a browser, while giving them higher App permissions means they can do things like create always-on-top windows, listen for global keyboard shortcuts, and send notifications. Full computer access means apps can run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time.

made some example apps available to try and to give users an idea of what's possible.



Anthropic says building an app and any calls it makes to Claude count toward usage limits. The feature remains in beta and is available on all plans in Claude Desktop, though Enterprise users will need to switch it on manually first.

title: Black Friday iPhone Duo deals: Your best chance to get one
content:
Macworld





The iPhone Duo is definitely making waves as Apple’s first foldable phone. Some users just have to have one and are looking at Black Friday sales in hopes of finding a discount. It is, after all, Apple’s most expensive iPhone ever.
Because the iPhone Duo is in such short supply, it can be difficult to find one in stock at all and even harder to find any sort of discount. Here are the best places to look.
Direct from Apple
Apple’s physical stores get in a small amount of stock regularly, but it’s impossible to predict it ahead of time, and they’re gone in a flash. See “stock tracking services” below to try to get an upper hand on it.
You can buy an iPhone Duo from Apple online, and the delivery estimate has gotten a lot better in recent days. Apple’s online store used to say to expect delivery in late January; now it’s saying 4-5 weeks or December 23 to January 5 for most orders. Some users report getting their order earlier than estimated. So there’s a chance you’ll still get your iPhone Duo before Christmas, if that’s your concern.
Big-box stores
Stores like Best Buy and Walmart seem to have limited stock, but there are some caveats. Only certain configurations are listed as ready to ship, typically those with more storage (and a higher price). They also require activating a new line on a carrier for which the store has a deal, typically T-Mobile, AT&T, or Verizon. Then you can pay the full price up front, or pay in monthly installments for several years. 
These are very nearly the same deals as buying direct from carrier stores, which you’ll find below. With limited stock available, it may be your preferred option.
Carrier deals
Carriers offer the “deals” on new iPhones every year, and they all take the same general setup: You have to activate a line on the carrier, and you have to buy the phone in monthly installments for usually 24 to 36 months. Your big discount comes in the form of bill credits toward those monthly installments. It’s common for carriers to limit these deals only to those who are on more premium phone plans, and some require you to trade in an eligible device.
In other words, it’s a way to lock you in to an expensive carrier plan for two or three years. If you leave the carrier or switch to a cheaper, unsupported plan, you’re on the hook for the remainder of the full phone price.
AT&T: No configurations shipping until January when we checked the website. The deal is $1,200 off as monthly bill credits for 36 months, with a qualifying trade-in.
Verizon: Verizon is currently showing delivery times in mid-December. The company offers “free” Apple Watch SE 3 & AirPods 5, as bill credits over 36 months, and you need a service plan for that Apple Watch.
T-Mobile: Current orders show that they’re shipping in January, and you get up to $2,100 of your purchase back as monthly bill credits. Only certain plans qualify.
In addition to the “big three” U.S. carriers, many of the MVNOs that use their networks (such as Xfinity, Mint Mobile, Boost Mobile, and others) offer the iPhone Duo for purchase, and some even have financing deals like the major carriers. They appear to be largely out of stock as well, with ship times estimated in mid-December through January.
Stock-tracking services
Whenever there is anything in short supply, you’ll find websites and services that will look for it to become in stock and notify you so you can jump on the purchase right away. Event tickets, sneakers, game consoles, you name it.
There are quite a lot of stock-checking sites that promise to be the very best choice for locating an iPhone Duo. (Believe me, we’ve gotten emails from all of them asking to be listed in our articles.) Here’s a sampling of them. We don’t have any way of knowing which is actually “the best,” and their inclusion here is not an official endorsement. This is just a sampling to get you started if you want to use such a service.
iPhoneStockChecker shows you nearby stock in various colors and storage sizes. 
OrionChime has two sub-sites. The one we are interested in checks stock for Apple products like iPhones, Mac Studio, or Mac mini.
Apple Inventory Check also checks inventory for various Apple products, including Macs and Apple Watch, and of course iPhones (including Duo). It’s limited to Apple Stores, but it’s faster than using the interface on Apple’s site to check availability of various configurations.
TrackaLacker is a general stock-tracking site for online retailers. You can watch iPhone Duo there, but only for the online stores of places like Best Buy or Walmart, not the Apple Store online or in-store stock.
InStock Tracker tracks all sorts of products, including iPhones.
Best Black Friday iPhone deals
Buying an iPhone from the U.K.? If it doesn’t have to be an iPhone Duo you can save hundreds on a new iPhone at Amazon right now. Here are our picks of the best Black Friday iPhone deals.

title: Tidal Bans AI Music, While Apple Music Sticks to Labels
content:
Streaming music service Tidal today said it plans to start blocking AI music on December 9. Any track generated entirely with AI will be removed from the platform, with Tidal rejecting AI songs in the future.


Tidal lead Robert Andersen said 43 percent of tracks uploaded in the last 90 days have been flagged as AI-generated. Approximately 29 million songs will be deleted and Tidal expects 80,000 to 85,000 songs to be rejected per day.

AI music will start disappearing on December 9 and will be "completely gone" at the beginning of 2027. AI-assisted music will continue to be allowed, since the policy is only for songs made entirely with AI tools. Tidal previously demonetized AI music, but removing it goes a step further.

Andersen said Tidal believes the move will "resonate with both artists and listeners alike" because 96 percent of AI songs get zero plays.

Apple Music, but it introduced AI Transparency Tags earlier this year. Apple is relying on labels and distributors to disclose when AI has been used, and it said in August that tracks "materially generated using AI" must have a "Made With AI" label.

title: Add Holiday Lights and Snow to Your Mac With Festivitas
content:
Festivitas is a fun little holiday-themed Mac app that developer Simon Støvring introduced two years ago and has been updating since. Its main purpose is to add lights to the Mac's Dock and menu bar, but there's also a version for the iPhone and iPad.


The holiday 2026 Festivitas update adds new customizations. For the first time, you can upload custom bulb shapes. There's an option to import an image and convert it to a bulb in a string of lights. Simple PNGs on a transparent background produce the best results, and for more complex images, bulbs can use the original colors.

You can customize light shapes, color, size, opacity, drop height, cable thickness, and more in the Settings. Lights can animate with different patterns, like pulse, twinkle, chase, and wave.

There are pointer decorations like sparkles, bubbles, falling leaves, confetti, a Christmas tree, a wreath, and more. Falling snow will now pile up on top of app windows for an added holiday effect. You can adjust snow rate, density, and flake size.

Snow and lights can be displayed above app windows or just on the desktop, with lights also visible on the Dock. Shortcuts can be used to play music and turn on lights, activate the snow effect if the weather forecast includes snow, and start a snowstorm.

Along with custom bulb shapes and falling snow, Festivitas for the iPhone and ‌iPad‌ now fully transparent animated widgets on the without a screenshot workaround.

Festivitas for Mac requires some accessibility access to work. I asked Støvring about Apple's planned permission changes in macOS 27.3, and how they will affect the Festivitas app. He said Festivitas gets far more access than it needs because Apple's options aren't granular enough, and he'd prefer to ask for less access.

Menu bar lights, snow, and pointer effects work without the System & App Protection Override permission, while lights in the Dock and snow landing on windows require access.

downloaded from the Festivitas website. The iPhone and ‌iPad‌ app is available for free from the App Store, and it too offers customer-selected fair pricing between $3.99 and $9.99. The updates are free for existing users. [Direct Link]
