title: Report: Product(RED) comes to two new Apple products next week
content:
Macworld





Apple has a longstanding tradition of supporting the Product(RED) cause, in which manufacturers create products in a very specific red color scheme, with a portion of the proceeds from those products go toward international charities that fight HIV and AIDS. However, it’s been a while since Apple sold a product in a Product(RED) colorway, and we assumed the partnership had run its course.
That’s not the case. Bloomberg reports that on or around December 1, Apple will introduce two new Product (RED) products for the first time in years. They will be the AirPods Max 2, in silver with a red digital crown, and an all-red HomePod mini 2. While Apple previously sold a silver version of the AirPods Max, the latest version released in April does not include a silver option. 
The Product(RED) campaign was started in 2006 by Bono and Bobby Shriver, and Apple was one of the first companies on board. It has been several years since the last Product(RED) offering from Apple: 2022’s iPhone 14 and 2023’s Apple Watch Series 9 were the last to be offered in Product(RED). A few iPhone cases were available for a short time after that.
Product(RED) Apple products don’t cost more than any other color, and these should be on shelves in time for the holidays. So if you like red, hold off on buying a new Homepod mini or AirPods Max for another week.
creator: Macworld

title: This dual-lens solar security camera just hit a new low for Black Friday
content:
Macworld





		
NEW LOWEST PRICE
Baseus U2 Pro Solar Outdoor Security Camera
View Deal
These days, it’s easier than ever to upgrade your home security, giving you the peace of mind of always being able to check in on your home, no matter where you are. For Black Friday, the Baseus U2 Pro is on sale for $118.99, a new all-time low price, down from its regular $150.
The U2 Pro sets itself part from standard outdoor security cameras with its dual-camera design and built-in solar panel. This one pairs a 3K fixed lens with an auto-tracking pan-tilt-zoom camera, giving you full 360-degree coverage of your entire yard. That basically means one camera that will never miss your driveway, even as the second camera turns and follows a suspicious person walking on your lawn. It also has a built-in spotlight that makes for clear video capture at night.
But it’s the built-in solar panel that makes this such a great camera for lazy or busy homeowners. Not only is the camera fully wireless, but that solar panel means it’ll never go dark during a power outage. And with its 7,800mAh battery, it just needs a few hours of direct sunlight on most days (not every day) to stay topped up and on the lookout.
That does come with some trade-offs though. Since it’s battery-powered, don’t expect 24/7 continuous recording; it uses motion sensors and triggers to know when it should record events. If you’re in a lot of shade or in an area with low sunlight, it may not stay topped up reliably. And while it can record footage locally on a microSD card, it does not offer a cloud storage plan.
If you just want a set-it-and-forget-it outdoor security camera with extensive coverage, and if you can mount it in a spot with lots of direct sunlight, the Baseus U2 Pro is a solid pick for $119 (was $150).

title: Best time to buy an iPhone in 2026: Should you buy now or wait?

Macworld





One of the best times to buy an iPhone is upon us: Black Friday week is here, and some of the deals are already live ahead of November 27. In the U.K., we’ve seen the unlocked 256GB iPhone Air for £799 at Amazon, £300 below Apple’s price and we are also seeing fantastic deals on the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. In the U.S., the biggest advertised savings often come from carriers. Compare what you’ll pay over the full term, factoring in the required plan and the value of any phone you trade in. If you’ve found a strong deal on the model and storage you want, there’s no need to wait until Friday. 
Alternatively, you may wish to consider Apple’s Black Friday offer. From November 27 to 30, it will offer a $100/£80 Apple Gift Card with an eligible iPhone Air purchase, $75/£60 with an iPhone 17 or iPhone 16, and $50/£40 with an iPhone 17e. The gift card goes toward a future Apple purchase, while a retailer discount saves you money at checkout. The iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo are excluded from Apple’s offer.
If you want an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, both are already here, so buy when the price or carrier offer works for you. The discontinued iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max are worth considering if you find stock at a meaningful saving over the equivalent 18 Pro. If you’re eyeing the iPhone Duo, check delivery times and read up on the early reports about its inner display. If you’d prefer the standard iPhone 18 or a next-generation iPhone Air, both are rumored for spring 2027.
Below, we explain which iPhones are worth buying now, which upcoming models might be worth waiting for, and when you’re most likely to find the best deals.

The worst time to buy an iPhone
This is generally in the weeks leading up to Apple’s September launch event, or in the early spring, when new models are expected to be announced. Buying just before a refresh means you could miss out on new features or pay full price for a model that’s about to be superseded.
The best time to buy an iPhone 
This depends on where you live:
In the U.K., where most iPhones are sold unlocked and off contract, the biggest savings are typically available during major sales events such as Amazon Prime Day (usually in July and October, and occasionally in March) and Black Friday in late November. However, worthwhile iPhone discounts can be found throughout the year if you know where to look.
In the U.S., where people tend to buy iPhones through a carrier, the best time to upgrade is often during Black Friday when networks enhance their offers with larger trade-in values, bill credits, gift cards, or discounted service plans. 
Due to the Black Friday sales, November and December could be a particularly good time to grab a deal on an older iPhone, such as the iPhone 17 Pro or iPhone 17 Pro Max. 








Should you buy a new iPhone now or wait? 

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




September and the months that follow are a much better time to buy an iPhone than earlier in the summer (July and August are usually poor months to buy a Pro iPhone because Apple’s September launch is so close). The iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo have now been unveiled, removing that uncertainty.
If you need a phone now, there’s little reason to wait for another annual refresh, and the iPhone 17, 17e and Air are also relatively safe purchases because their successors aren’t expected until spring 2027. See: iPhone 18 and 18e rumors and iPhone Air 2 rumors. 
The iPhone 17 remains the strongest value, with a 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage for $899/£899 (although it was previously $799/£799). The 18 Pro and Pro Max make more sense if you want the best cameras, performance or battery life, while the Duo is for buyers specifically interested in Apple’s new folding design.
There is, however, one important reason to wait: 2027 could bring a much bigger iPhone redesign. Apple is rumored to be preparing a 20th-anniversary iPhone – the iPhone 19 or 20 with a near-all-screen curved design, under-display Face ID, possible solid-state buttons, a thinner and more efficient OLED display, a larger battery and major camera improvements. That could make 2027 a more significant upgrade year than 2026.
So if your current iPhone is still serving you well, waiting could be worthwhile. If you need a phone now, and especially if you find a deal in the Black Friday sales, it’s a good time to buy one. 
Wondering which iPhone to buy? Read: Best iPhone for our ranked recommendations and our iPhone buying guide for more in-depth information about cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Should you wait for the iPhone 18?
For most people, there isn’t a strong reason to wait for the iPhone 18. Apple isn’t expected to launch the standard model until spring 2027, so buying an iPhone 17 before the end of 2026 would still give you several months with Apple’s current mainstream model before its replacement arrives.
The iPhone 18 is expected to bring a 2nm A20 chip, potentially 9GB or 12GB of RAM, Apple’s C2 modem and possibly a new 24MP front camera. Extra RAM could prove particularly useful for future Apple Intelligence and Siri features. However, the rear camera system is still expected to consist of two 48MP cameras, while the display may remain broadly similar to the iPhone 17’s 6.3-inch ProMotion panel.
There is also some uncertainty over exactly what the iPhone 18 lineup will look like. A September 2026 rumour suggested Apple could effectively merge the standard iPhone and iPhone Air into a single model, rather than continuing them as two separate devices. If that happens, the iPhone 18 could adopt some of the Air’s thinner, lighter design while retaining the broader appeal of the standard iPhone. For now, though, that remains speculative.
Price is another consideration. With the arrival of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, Apple increased iPhone prices across the range, so the iPhone 17 now costs $899, $100 more than at launch. When the iPhone 18 arrives, it is likely to inherit that $899 price point, while the iPhone 17 could drop back to around $799 at which you may regret buying it at the higher price.
Wait if you want the newer A20 chip, potentially more RAM, an improved front camera, or are intrigued by the possibility of a thinner redesigned standard model. 
Don’t wait if you simply want ProMotion, dual 48MP cameras, excellent battery life and 256GB of storage as standard – the iPhone 17 already delivers all of that.

 FAQ 


1.
When is the best carrier upgrade timing? 
Apple typically announces new iPhone models in September. Carriers often roll out their most aggressive trade-in offers and promotional deals around this time to entice customers to upgrade.
New releases: Waiting for the September (or spring) launch window is generally a good strategy if you want the latest model at a potentially better subsidized price.
Check your contract cycle: Many carrier contracts today last 24 to 36 months. If you’re nearing the end of your contract, you’re in a strong position to negotiate or take advantage of upgrade offers. However, upgrading mid-contract may involve paying off the remaining balance, so it’s worth checking your specific terms.
Consider Apple’s upgrade plans: Apple has replaced its old iPhone Upgrade Program with newer financing and leasing options. In the U.S., Apple Upgrade lets you lease an iPhone through Klarna and upgrade, buy or return it at the end of the term. In the U.K., Apple’s Flexible Finance Account offers eligible iPhones on monthly payment plans with the option to upgrade after a set number of payments. Terms and monthly costs vary by model.





2.
When does Apple update the iPhone?
Apple typically unveils new iPhones at a dedicated Apple event in September. Preorders usually open the following Friday, with devices shipping and arriving in stores a week later. However, some models arrive later: Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and iPhone Duo in September 2026, but the Pro models went on sale September 18, while the Duo followed on October 23.
Apple also launches iPhones earlier in the year, particularly its more affordable models. The iPhone 16e arrived in February 2025 and the iPhone 17e in March 2026. The standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 are expected in spring 2027.
These spring launches are often announced via press release, although Apple has also held spring events. Availability typically follows within one to two weeks, but initial supplies can be limited.
Compatible iPhones also receive a major iOS update each year, usually in September, bringing new features that can give an older phone a fresh lease of life.
Read our guide to the next Apple event to find out what’s coming next.





3.
When do iPhone prices drop and by how much?
Based on past experience, Apple is very unlikely to reduce the price of a new iPhone during its first year on sale.
However, when Apple introduces a new generation of iPhones, it usually cuts the price of the previous year’s models. That means September has traditionally been the point when older iPhones become cheaper.
Apple also tends to keep launch prices broadly similar from one generation to the next, at least in the U.S., although exchange rates and other regional factors can affect pricing elsewhere.
In 2024, for example, Apple reduced the price of the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Plus by $100/£100 when the iPhone 16 and 16 Plus arrived. The iPhone 16 also fell in price following the launch of the iPhone 17 in 2025. However, because the iPhone 17 doubled the base storage to 256GB, the older iPhone 16 looked less attractive even at $100/£100 less.
In 2026, the pattern changed. Apple actually raised iPhone prices, blaming higher memory costs. Even the year-old iPhone 17 and two-year-old iPhone 16 increased by $100, showing that older iPhones don’t always become cheaper when a new generation arrives.





4.
Is it better to buy from Apple or a carrier?
In the U.S., buying from Apple is usually the better option if you value flexibility. If you pay in full or use Apple’s own financing, the iPhone is unlocked, so you can switch carriers or use another eSIM when traveling. Apple also accepts trade-ins and, importantly, many AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon promotions are available when buying through Apple.
However, an iPhone bought from Apple but financed through an AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon device-payment plan is locked to that carrier until it has been paid off. An iPhone bought outright from Apple isn’t.
The main reason to buy directly from AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon is to take advantage of a particularly good promotion. U.S. carriers frequently advertise large trade-in credits or “free” iPhones, especially when you add a line or switch networks. The catch is that the discount is usually provided as monthly bill credits over 24 or 36 months, so if you leave early you can lose the remaining credits.
In the U.K., Apple sells iPhones unlocked and SIM-free, allowing you to shop separately for a SIM-only plan from EE, Vodafone, O2, Three or an MVNO. This makes it easier to switch networks and can work out cheaper over the life of the phone than bundling the handset and airtime into a single contract.
Apple isn’t necessarily the cheapest place to buy, however. Amazon U.K. and other retailers frequently discount SIM-free iPhones, and there can be substantial savings during sales events such as Black Friday.
Networks can also offer compelling promotions, including enhanced trade-in values, discounted airtime, generous data allowances or lower monthly payments. But make sure you compare the total cost of the contract, rather than focusing on the headline monthly price.





5.
When are the best iPhone deals?
The earliest you could expect to get a discount on the newest iPhones is around Black Friday at the end of November, so you might be planning to hold out until then. However, the deals we tend to see, if any, are usually for older handsets. See our round-up of Best Black Friday iPhone deals for more.
Nor should you expect to get a discount in an Apple Black Friday sale. Apple’s Black Friday sale usually only takes the form of vouchers with select product purchases, rather than a discount, and it is unlikely that the newest iPhone would qualify as in previous year’s new iPhones haven’t been included. 
Note that while shopping events like Black Friday get all the attention, that’s not the only time you can get discounts on Apple products: we see discounts all the time. Another event where we see good iPhone deals is Prime Day, which happens in June or July and October every year. So take a look at the iPhone deals for Amazon Prime Day sale to see what you might be able to save.
In our experience, we don’t tend to see discounts on the newest handset until the spring – and these are always from third-party resellers, never from Apple. In fact, we don’t tend to see the iPhone discounted in the U.S. very often, most of the discounts we see are in the U.K. where unlocked iPhones are often sold off-contract at a good discount.





6.
Is it worth buying a refurbished iPhone? 
Yes, buying a refurbished iPhone is absolutely worth it for most people, especially if you want to save money without sacrificing quality. 
Buying refurbished is a great way to “pick up a bargain” while still getting a premium device. You can typically save 15% to 30% compared to buying new, and sometimes much more on older models. 
A common misconception is that refurbished is the same as buying a used phone from a stranger, though. It’s not. A used phone is sold “as-is,” with no guarantee it will work properly. A refurbished phone has been professionally inspected, tested, and repaired if needed, and it comes with a warranty. 
If you want the highest quality, Apple’s own refurbished store is the gold standard.





7.
How to check iPhone stock near you

title: This insane trick turns the MacBook’s trackpad into a speaker
content:
Macworld





The next time you’re sitting next to a PC fanboy droning on and on about how much MacBooks suck (seriously, I work with a bunch of them), here’s a little trick you can do to shut them up. It’s a demo created by developer Cody Collier, and it makes the Force Touch Trackpad on a MacBook play sounds rather than just vibration buzzes. It uses the trackpad’s haptic engine to make a robot-like voice and tunes that sound like they’re from a 1970s video game.
The demo is called No Speaker, and it’s available on GitHub for free. The program takes the haptic engine and “drives that motor up to 4,000 times a second, fast enough to make sound you can hear, and turns it into a voice.” To run the demo, you must have a MacBook with a Force Touch Trackpad (2015 and later MacBooks) or a Magic Trackpad 2 or newer. You also need macOS 12 or later on Apple Silicon, or macOS 13 or later on Intel. That’s a long list of Macs, so I’m sure yours will qualify.
The GitHub site has simple instructions for downloading and running the demo. All you need to do is open the Terminal, and then copy and paste this prompt: curl -fsSL a90.com/nospeaker | sh and it will install and run the demo. You need to mute your Mac’s actual speakers; the demo will tell you to do so. Be warned: When I played the demo, it was pretty loud and you can’t turn it down. To stop the demo, you need to quit the Terminal. Check out Collier’s demo video below to hear No Speaker in action.


i made my macbook trackpad talk using only the vibrations from its haptic motor 
my speakers are muted, every sound you hear is coming from the trackpad itself
open source, try it here: https://t.co/MPEKltkFxO pic.twitter.com/5rTtqdErDP
— cody (@codycollier) November 22, 2026





No Speaker is a self-contained demo, so it only plays what goes through the demo app. You can type in words and hear them through the trackpad as well as adjust the pitch and vibrato by sliding your finger along the surface. But if you open the Music app to play a song in an attempt to play it through the trackpad, it won’t work.
The demo itself has a robotic voice, and the music is like the 8-bit tone of early video games, simple and basic. No Speaker’s tones are a bit jarring because it demonstrates how high the pitch reaches.
How is Collier able to make sound through the trackpad? The trackpad doesn’t have a speaker, so the demo takes the haptic engine and vibrates the glass in the trackpad fast enough that it makes sound. While this does seem a bit risky to the functionality of the trackpad, Collier states on GitHub that No Speaker “never drives the motor past its normal maximum strength. Going past it is possible and louder, but the driver starts to stall.” He says No Speaker doesn’t do that, but it’s not a direct statement saying it’s completely safe, so you probably don’t want to play the demo often.
Still, it’s just one more way to show how much cooler your MacBook is than a Windows laptop.

title: Developer Turns MacBook Trackpad Into a Speaker Using Haptic Motor
content:
A new free tool makes a MacBook's Force Touch trackpad produce speech and music by vibrating its glass, even when the computer's speakers are muted.


The open-source project is called "NO SPEAKER," and comes from developer Cody Collier, who recently shared shared a demonstration on X. The tool uses the small haptic motor that normally makes a Force Touch trackpad feel as though it clicks. Driving that motor at different frequencies makes the glass vibrate fast enough to produce audible sounds.

The demo lasts around a minute and a half and includes speech, a melody, a beat, and a short rap. Users can also slide a finger across the trackpad to change the pitch of a tone, enter their own text for it to speak, or choose another installed macOS voice. The tool does not turn the trackpad into a normal audio output for playing music files or sound from other apps.

i made my macbook trackpad talk using only the vibrations from its haptic motor
my speakers are muted, every sound you hear is coming from the trackpad itself
open source, try it here: github.com/os6/nospeaker
— cody (@codycollier) November 22, 2026



To generate speech, the software starts with a voice created by macOS's built-in text-to-speech feature. It breaks the recording into tiny sections and picks out the main sound frequencies that make the words recognizable. The motor then reproduces a simplified version of those sounds through the trackpad.

The result is a quiet, robotic voice. Collier says the words are easier to follow when reading the text displayed alongside them, and recommends placing the MacBook on a table to make the sound easier to hear.

The tool uses parts of macOS that Apple does not make available for third-party developers to use, namely the "MultitouchSupport" framework. These let it control how fast and strongly the trackpad vibrates, rather than simply trigger a preset click. Since Apple does not officially support this use-case, a future macOS update could stop the tool from working.

available now on GitHub.

title: Apple Wallet Driver's License Feature Coming to Connecticut
content:
Starting next year, residents of Connecticut will be able to add their driver's license or state ID to the Apple Wallet app on the iPhone and Apple Watch. The digital ID can be used to display proof of identity or age at TSA checkpoints in select airports, at select businesses, and in select iPhone apps, but acceptance is still very limited.


Last week, Connecticut released a mobile ID app on iOS and Android, and the app's developer IDEMIA said Apple Wallet, Google Wallet, and Samsung Wallet support will be "coming soon." In a May 2026 press release, Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont's office said it aimed to  support the trio of digital wallets "by August 2027."

in September 2021, Apple announced that Connecticut had "signed up" to offer driver's licenses and state IDs in the Apple Wallet app, but more than five years have passed and nothing has materialized. With a goal of August 2027 now in place, though, the functionality should finally be available next year.

16 other U.S. states have rolled out Apple Wallet IDs so far: Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Virginia, and West Virginia. The feature is also available in Puerto Rico and works with Japan's My Number Card.

in North Carolina and Utah over the coming months, and years ago it announced that Kentucky and Mississippi were committed to launching the feature at some point.

To set up the feature, open the Wallet app on the iPhone and tap on the plus sign in the top-right corner. Next, tap on Driver's License and ID Cards, select your state from the list, and follow the on-screen steps to complete the process. Then, you can present your digital ID where it is accepted without handing over your device.

You can present an Apple Wallet ID where accepted by simply tapping your iPhone or Apple Watch on an identity reader. Then, you will be able to view the specific information being requested by the TSA or business. Only after authorizing with Face ID or Touch ID is the requested identity information released from your device.

As mentioned, you do not need to unlock, show, or hand over your device to present an Apple Wallet ID in person, ensuring user privacy.

Apple Wallet IDs are accepted at TSA checkpoints in more than 250 airports across the U.S. for domestic travel, according to Apple.

title: Coalition of 55,000 EU Businesses Challenges Apple
content:
Mozilla, Shopify, and a coalition representing up to 55,000 European Union businesses and organizations are urging the European Commission to take enforcement action against Apple over restrictions on competing iPhone browsers.


In an open letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the coalition argues that Apple's changes under the Digital Markets Act (DMA) have failed to deliver meaningful browser competition. According to organizer Open Web Advocacy, no browser vendor has been able to switch its existing EU users from Apple's WebKit engine to its own engine more than two and a half years after Apple's compliance deadline. Signatories include Vivaldi, Vercel, Y Combinator, the European DIGITAL SME Alliance, European Publishers Council, News Media Europe, and European Digital Rights. 

began allowing alternative browser engines in the EU with iOS 17.4, but the coalition says its conditions make that permission impractical to use. Browser engines power websites and web apps, determining their performance and available features.

outlined the problem in a separate statement on November 20. It says bringing its Gecko engine to iOS would require releasing a second Firefox app rather than updating the existing one. Users would then have to download that app, transfer their bookmarks, passwords, and history, and switch manually.

requirements say competing engines must meet privacy and security standards, including timely vulnerability fixes. The company says these conditions protect users from malicious web content.

title: Best MacBook for 2026: Air vs Pro vs Neo compared
content:
Macworld





Apple sells several MacBook models across different sizes, prices, and performance levels, so choosing the right one depends on your budget, the type of work you do, and how much power you actually need.
In this in-depth guide, we explain which MacBook is best for different users, compare the latest MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and the MacBook Pro models (with and without touchscreen), and help you decide how much RAM and how much storage you really need.
Choosing a MacBook Pro now involves two decisions: how much processing power you need, and which display you want. The entry-level 14-inch model uses the M6 chip, while more demanding users can choose M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations with either a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display or a PROLED XDR OLED touchscreen.
For most people, the MacBook Air remains our recommended starting point. If you need a Pro, choose the chip, memory and storage around your workload, then consider whether the touchscreen model’s OLED display and lighter design justify the extra cost. In this article, we’ll help you decide whether a MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, or MacBook Neo is the best fit for your needs.
If you’re buying during Black Friday week, check our best Black Friday MacBook deals and compare prices for the same memory and storage before choosing between the Air and Pro.

Which MacBook is right for you?
In 2026, Apple’s laptop lineup spans five main choices: the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, the mainstream MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro, the high-performance M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro and the touchscreen versions of those MacBook Pro models.
Best for basic use and tight budgets: MacBook Neo is ideal for students, casual browsing, streaming, and light productivity at the lowest entry price.
Best for most people: MacBook Air (M5)  offers the best mix of portability, battery life, silent operation, and everyday performance.
Best for those who want a superior display and extra ports: The MacBook Pro (M6) offers professional-grade features without the extreme power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. 
Best for professionals and power users: MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max) is best for demanding workflows such as 4K video editing, 3D work, heavy multitasking, and software development.
Best for high-end creative professionals: Suited to those who work extensively on their laptop’s built-in display and need direct touch interaction.

The MacBook Air (M5) is the best MacBook for most buyers because it offers the strongest balance of price, portability, battery life, and performance.
The 13-inch MacBook Air is light, quiet, fast enough for everyday work, and easier to recommend than any other Mac laptop. The latest version, updated in March 2026, keeps the same winning formula while improving storage and connectivity. There is also a 15-inch version for anyone who wants a larger screen. 
What’s new
The latest MacBook Air features the M5 chip, base storage is 512GB, and it supports newer wireless standards including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Why we recommend the MacBook Air
Excellent balance of performance and portability
Silent fanless design
Long battery life
Strong everyday performance for work, school, and travel
Now ships with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage as standard
Sizes
The MacBook Air comes in two sizes:
13-inch MacBook Air, 13.6-inch screen: Best for portability
15-inch MacBook Air, 15.3-inch screen: Better for multitasking and split-screen work
Display
As you can see from the above measurements, the display, when measured diagonally is a little larger than the standard naming would suggest. As a result the 13-inch MacBook Air display is actually larger than that on the 13-inch MacBook Neo, discussed below. The MacBook Air uses a bright Liquid Retina display, but it still lacks the 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and HDR capabilities found on MacBook Pro models.
Performance
The M5 chip in the MacBook Air is fast enough for office work, school tasks, web apps, multitasking, and light creative work. Because the Air has no fan, though, performance can dip during long video exports or other sustained heavy workloads so that the temperature remains optimal.
Battery life
Battery life is excellent, making the Air a great choice for anyone who works away from a desk. It offers more battery life than the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, but falls short of the 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Other specs
You get MagSafe 3 for charging and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The MacBook Air also supports up to two external displays. (Older M1 and M2 models were limited to one external monitor). 
16GB RAM to 32GB RAM

Price
Apple put MacBook Air prices up by $200 in June 2026.

15-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,499/£1,499
What to know before buying
The Air’s biggest limitation is sustained performance. It is quick for most tasks, but it is not the right machine for users who regularly push their system for long periods. The MacBook Air is likely to soon adopt the M6 chip as used in the entry-level MacBook Pro, Mac mini and iMac.

The MacBook Neo is the cheapest way to buy a Mac laptop in 2026. Now starting at $699 (which is unfortunately $100 more than it was when Apple launched it in March), it is aimed at students, first-time Mac buyers, and casual users who mainly browse the web, stream video, join video calls, and work in basic apps.
Despite its lower price, it still looks and feels like a MacBook, with an all-aluminum design and a lightweight chassis.
Who is MacBook Neo for?
The MacBook Neo is best for people whose computing needs are simple: web browsing, email, documents, streaming, and schoolwork.
Why we recommend MacBook Neo
Lowest price in the lineup
Light and portable
Quiet fanless design
Good battery life
Fast enough for basic everyday use
Sizes
The MacBook Neo comes in just one size:
13-inch MacBook Neo, 13-inch screen
Display 
Like the MacBook Air the MacBook Neo offers a Liquid Retina display with max 500 nits brightness, but that’s where the similarities end. The display is slightly smaller than the display on the 13-inch MacBook Air, offering 2,408 by 1,506 pixels compared to 2,560 by 1,664 pixels. It also lacks the wide color P3 and True Tone technology of the other MacBooks, offering only sRGB color. 
Performance 
The MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip – the same processor first introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro. While it is a mobile-class chip, its performance is optimized for a laptop environment, offering a highly responsive experience for everyday productivity. In our tests it proved faster than the M3 in single-core, while equal to the M1 when it came to multi-core performance and graphics. 
Battery life 
The MacBook Neo should comfortably last a working day of general productivity. In our video-loop battery test, with screen brightness set to 150 nits, it lasted 13 hours and 15 minutes. Apple advertises up to 16 hours of video streaming or 11 hours of wireless web browsing. More demanding tasks will drain the battery faster.
Other specs
You get two USB-C ports, but these are not identical in capability, one being USB 3 and the other USB 2. See MacBook Neo ports explained. The MacBook Neo only supports one external display with a resolution of up to 4K at 60Hz.

What to know before buying
The Neo makes several trade-offs to achieve its low price, including the absence of a backlit keyboard, a limited selection of ports, and no Touch ID on the base model. It also features a lower-quality display compared to the Air and Pro, offers less memory with a maximum of 8GB RAM, and delivers lower sustained performance than M-series MacBooks. For many buyers, the 512GB, $799 model represents better value, as it includes Touch ID and additional storage.
Alternatives
The MacBook Neo is the best budget MacBook, but it is best suited to light workloads. If you can spend more, the MacBook Air remains the better long-term buy for most people.
Another option, if a low price is your top priority, is a refurbished MacBook. Look out for clearance deals on older Apple silicon MacBooks, but avoid the older Intel-based models. See: MacBook Pro deals and MacBook Air deals.

Performance
The M6 has a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU. Choose it for everyday work and creative projects; consider M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations when you need greater graphics or memory capacity. In our tests, the M6 MacBook Pro scored 16 percent higher in Geekbench 7 multicore and 23 percent higher in Metal graphics compute than the previous M5 MacBook Pro. It also completed our 4K video export 30 percent faster. That makes it a good step up for occasional video editing, while the M5 Pro and M5 Max are better suited to heavier production workloads.
Battery life
Apple rates it for up to 24 hours of video streaming or 16 hours of wireless web browsing. Actual endurance depends on your workload. In our test, the M6 MacBook Pro lasted 27.5 hours looping a locally stored 4K video at 150 nits, only a few minutes longer than the M5 MacBook Pro.

What to know before buying
The combination of OLED, touch and reduced weight may justify the premium if you regularly work on the built-in screen. If you mainly use an external monitor, a non-touchscreen model could offer better value.

Our reviewer Roman Loyola praised its brightness, richer colors and deeper blacks, making it an appealing upgrade even if you prefer using the keyboard and trackpad. Touch is a useful addition, but you don’t need to use it to appreciate the better display.

							
		


MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
The M5 MacBook Air and M6 MacBook Pro are different in some significant ways.

Foundry




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work and light creative projects in a thin, light, silent design. Choose the MacBook Pro if you regularly run demanding workloads or will benefit from its better display and additional ports.
The closest comparison is between the M5 MacBook Air and 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. For more demanding professional work, the MacBook Pro also offers M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with a choice of non-touchscreen or PROLED XDR touchscreen displays.
Performance: Do you need a MacBook Pro?
The M5 MacBook Air is well suited to web browsing, office apps, studying, photo editing, and occasional video projects. Using creative software doesn’t automatically mean you need a Pro: the size of your projects and how frequently you run demanding tasks matter more.
The M6 MacBook Pro combines a newer chip generation with active cooling. Its fans help it sustain performance during lengthy video exports, code compilation, and other intensive tasks. The Air’s fanless design keeps it completely silent, but performance can fall during prolonged heavy workloads.
If these demanding tasks make up much of your working day, consider an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. These offer greater processing, graphics, and memory capacity than the standard M6 model. A newer chip generation doesn’t automatically make the M6 the more powerful choice.
Display and ports: What does the Pro add?
The MacBook Air’s Liquid Retina display is suitable for everyday work, with 500 nits brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. You can choose a 13-inch model for portability or a 15-inch model for more workspace.
The M6 MacBook Pro’s 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display adds mini-LED technology, deeper contrast, brighter HDR highlights, and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. These features are particularly useful for viewing and editing HDR content, although you don’t need to be a creative professional to appreciate the screen.
The M6 MacBook Pro also provides three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot. The Air has two Thunderbolt 4 ports, so connecting memory cards, HDMI displays, or several accessories may require adapters or a dock.
For an OLED touchscreen, choose a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Touchscreen availability is a separate consideration from how much processing power you need.
Portability, battery life, and price
The Air is thinner and lighter, making it the stronger choice if you carry your laptop regularly. The 15-inch Air is also worth considering if you want a larger screen without the weight and expense of a 16-inch Pro.
The M6 MacBook Pro has a higher advertised battery-life rating, although actual endurance depends on your workload. Both models are suitable for working away from a power socket.
The Air costs less, but compare configurations with matching memory and storage before deciding. The M6 MacBook Pro starts with more storage, which narrows the price difference if you would otherwise upgrade the Air.
Our buying advice: Air or Pro?
Buy the MacBook Air for everyday work, studying, travel, and light creative projects. It offers the best balance of performance, portability, and price for most buyers.
Buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you’ll use its HDR display and additional ports, and benefit from longer advertised battery life, or better sustained performance.
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro for demanding professional workloads that justify more processing power, graphics performance, or memory. Consider the PROLED XDR version if you also want OLED and touch.

While Windows PCs still hold a performance lead in raw frames per second, Apple Silicon has made high-end gaming a viable reality on macOS, particularly with the latest Pro and Max models. 
The M5 Pro MacBook Pro, updated in March 2026, strikes a balance for those who need “oomph” for gaming without the extreme price tag of the M5 Max version of the MacBook Pro. 
It includes Thunderbolt 5 ports for high-speed data transfer and supports more unified memory than the base M5. It is specifically recommended for “serious gaming” and moderate media production.
The M5 Pro model lacks the massive GPU core count of the Max chip, meaning it may struggle with the highest settings on the most demanding AAA titles like Cyberpunk 2077.
In our real-world gaming benchmarks, it provides “good results” for Mac users, even if it still faces a gap compared to dedicated PC gaming rigs.

Is MacBook Air good enough?

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Air may suffice in some cases: 
Creatives: The Air works well for light creative work, especially photo editing, design, and shorter video projects. It is not as strong in sustained workloads, but it is much easier to carry and costs less.
Development: The MacBook Air is still a good choice for lighter software development, especially for web development, scripting, and general programming. It is best for developers who prioritize portability over maximum sustained speed.
Gaming: The M5 MacBook Air features a third-generation ray-tracing engine and enhanced shader cores, which Apple says improves 3D rendering and gaming tasks. However, in our tests the lack of active cooling caused performance to dip after playing for 10 minutes or so. You can play casual games just fine, but for a variety of reasons, if you’re into AAA gaming, the Air isn’t the best choice.
What about MacBook Neo?
If your budget is much tighter and your needs are basic, the MacBook Neo is the entry point. It gives you macOS at a much lower price, but with more compromises than the Air. If you choose the Neo we recommend the 512GB version.

Other MacBook buying decisions to consider
When buying a MacBook, it’s important to consider how you will use it, as this will determine the right balance of performance, portability, and price. 
Key factors to consider include which chip you require, how much RAM you will need for multitasking, and the size of the SSD required for storage, all of which cannot be upgraded later. 
Screen size affects portability and productivity, screen quality is key for creative work, while battery life matters if you work on the go. You should also think about weight, port selection, and long-term value to ensure the device meets your needs both now and in the future.
In the next section we’ll examine these elements of the buying decision. 


						

							


Best MacBook display and screen size

The best MacBook screen size depends on how much portability, screen space, and display quality you need.
Best MacBook screen sizes
Best size for most people: 13-inch MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro
Best size for portability: 13-inch MacBook Air or MacBook Neo 
Best all-around Pro size: 14-inch MacBook Pro 
Best large-screen option without Pro pricing: 15-inch MacBook Air 
Best for maximum workspace: 16-inch MacBook Pro 
How many screens are supported 
The 13-inch and 14-inch MacBooks offer the best balance of portability and usability. The larger 15-inch and 16-inch options are ideal if you want more room for spreadsheets, side-by-side apps, or general multitasking. These displays can run alongside the built-in screen. The M5 Pro and M5 Max limits apply to both touchscreen and non-touchscreen models.
MacBook Neo: Supports only one external display up to 4K at 60Hz.
MacBook Air (M5): Supports up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M6): Supports up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M5 Pro): Supports up to three external displays, each at 6K/60Hz.
MacBook Pro (M5 Max): Supports up to four external displays, each at 6K/60Hz.
For more advice read: How to use two or more monitors to a Mac.
MacBook displays: Liquid Retina, Liquid Retina XDR and PROLED XDR
Apple’s MacBooks offer three main display types. The most useful differences are brightness, contrast, refresh rate and touchscreen support.
Liquid Retina: MacBook Neo and MacBook Air
These displays suit everyday work, web browsing and watching videos. They have a fixed 60Hz refresh rate and don’t support touch. The Air’s display also supports the wider P3 color gamut, making it a better choice than the Neo for color-sensitive work.
Liquid Retina XDR: Non-touchscreen MacBook Pro
The M6 MacBook Pro and non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use mini-LED displays. These offer higher contrast and brighter HDR highlights than the Air, plus ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother scrolling and motion.
PROLED XDR: Touchscreen MacBook Pro
The touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use OLED displays. OLED controls light at the individual pixel level, producing deep blacks without the backlight blooming that can occur with mini-LED. These models also support direct touchscreen input.

For most people, the Air’s display is sufficient. Choose a Liquid Retina XDR model if HDR brightness and ProMotion matter to your work. Consider PROLED XDR if you particularly value OLED’s contrast or want touchscreen input.


Is the touchscreen MacBook Pro worth paying extra for?
The touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $400/£400 more than an equivalent non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model. That premium buys display and design improvements, with the same processor options.
What the premium gets you
A tandem OLED display: The PROLED XDR screen offers higher contrast and adds Adobe RGB alongside P3 color support. This may be particularly valuable for photographers, video editors and designers who regularly use the built-in display.
Touchscreen input: Scroll, pinch to zoom and interact directly with content onscreen, alongside the keyboard and trackpad. Its usefulness will depend on your apps and how you prefer to work.
A thinner, lighter design: The 14-inch model weighs approximately half a pound less than its non-touch equivalent. Both sizes also replace the notch with Dynamic Island.
When it’s worth the extra money
The premium is easiest to justify if you spend much of your working day using the laptop’s own screen. The combination of OLED, wider color support and touch could make it a more useful workspace, while the reduced weight benefits anyone who frequently carries their MacBook.
You don’t have to want touch to appreciate the other improvements. As Macworld’s Roman Loyola argues, the display may be the more compelling upgrade.
When to choose a non-touch model
If you mainly work with an external monitor, the upgraded built-in display offers less benefit. A non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max can provide the processing power and memory you need at a lower price.
Touch also won’t suit every workflow. Reaching across the keyboard may be less comfortable than using the trackpad for extended periods, so consider how often you would actually use it.
Compare matching chip, memory and storage configurations before deciding: retailer discounts could make the price difference larger than $400/£400.


						

							


Which is the best MacBook for battery life?
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro share Apple’s highest advertised video-streaming rating, at up to 24 hours. For wireless web browsing, the 16-inch M5 Pro leads at up to 17 hours.
The MacBook Air offers a lighter, less expensive option, with both sizes rated for up to 18 hours of video streaming or 15 hours of web browsing. The budget-friendly MacBook Neo has lower advertised endurance, at 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively.
See: MacBook Air, Pro and Neo batteries compared.

How much RAM do you need?
For most buyers in 2026, 16GB of RAM should be the minimum. That is the sweet spot for a MacBook you plan to keep for several years. 
However, the MacBook Neo ships with only 8GB RAM, and there are no options to upgrade this capacity at the time of purchase or later. Whether this is enough RAM depends entirely on your specific use case, as the device is positioned as a budget-friendly entry point into the Mac ecosystem. For the target audience – students, teachers, and casual users – 8GB of RAM should be sufficient for general productivity. A significant concern regarding the 8GB capacity is its long-term viability. 
MacBook memory is not upgradeable after purchase. If you expect to keep your laptop for a long time, it is worth buying more RAM upfront if your budget allows.
RAM recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 16GB recommended. 8GB is workable for very light use, but not ideal for longevity.
Creative work and gaming: 24GB to 32GB is the safer target.
Professionals and AI-heavy workflows: 48GB to 128GB, depending on workload.

How much storage do you need for a MacBook?
256GB: Fine for cloud-first users with light local storage needs, but it can fill up quickly.
512GB: The better starting point for most people. It gives you more breathing room for apps, files, photos, and offline media.
1TB or more: Best for media professionals, developers with larger local workloads, or anyone who works with large files regularly.
Determining the best storage capacity for a MacBook depends heavily on your specific workflow, as internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase. 
While Apple previously offered 256GB as a baseline, most current models now start at 512GB or 1TB to accommodate the increasing space requirements of modern operating systems and applications. For most buyers, 512GB is the practical minimum if the budget allows.
Experts now generally advise against 256GB drives for primary machines. Furthermore, SSDs can slow down significantly as they fill up. A common rule of thumb is to buy at least twice the capacity of what you need to store to maintain performance.
Storage (SSD) recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 512GB recommended. Sufficient for documents, web browsing, and light media use.
General Productivity: 512GB to 1TB recommended. For users with moderate photo libraries and some video projects.
Creative Professionals: 1TB to 2TB+ recommended. Necessary for 4K video editing, large high-resolution photo libraries, and professional audio suites.
High-End Workflows: 4TB to 8TB recommended. For 3D animation, AI development, and massive video production projects.
Is there a difference between SSDs in Apple’s MacBooks
There are significant differences in SSD performance, capacity, and technology across the current MacBook lineup. In March 2026, Apple introduced faster storage technologies for the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models. 
The most notable differences lie in the read/write speeds, which vary based on the model’s processor and the physical capacity of the drive:
MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max): The M5 Pro and Max models, released in March 2026, feature the fastest internal storage in the lineup. Apple claims these SSDs are up to twice as fast as the previous generation. 
MacBook Pro (M6): Apple describes the SSD in the M6 model as “Superfast”. With the arrival of the M5 in 2025 Apple claimed it delivered up to 2x faster read/write performance than its predecessors.
MacBook Air (M5): The M5 MacBook Air also received a similar storage speed boost with the March 2026 update. 
MacBook Neo: The MacBook Neo uses a slower SSD to maintain its lower price point.

Which MacBook chip should you choose?
Choosing the right MacBook chip in 2026 depends on your specific workflow, ranging from basic productivity to high-end professional creative work. Apple’s current lineup features the M5 family (M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max) and the budget-friendly A18 Pro.
Apple’s MacBook chips currently fall into four clear tiers.

M5: Best for general users, students, and office work.
M5 Pro: Best for photographers, editors, programmers, and users with heavier workloads.

 FAQ 


1.
Which MacBook lasts the longest?
For battery life, the MacBook Pro models lead the lineup, with 24 hours of playback.





2.
Should I buy a refurbished MacBook?
A refurbished MacBook can be a good value, especially if you buy Apple silicon rather than Intel. Just make sure the price gap is meaningful and the machine still has enough life left to justify the purchase.
Since Apple put up prices across the range buying in the Refurbished Store is even more attractive. The MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro were all available at the original price shortly after Apple raised prices. 
For example, the MacBook Neo is $599, you can get a 13-inch, M5 MacBook Air for $1,099 and a 14-inch MacBook Pro, M5 Pro for $2,119.





3.
Is a MacBook Air powerful enough?
Yes. For most people, the MacBook Air is more than powerful enough for everyday work, school, multitasking, web use, and light creative tasks.





4.
Is a MacBook worth it compared to a Windows laptop?
That depends on your priorities, but MacBooks are often worth the extra cost if you value exceptional battery life, premium build quality, class-leading trackpads, and seamless integration with the Apple ecosystem.
Apple’s recent price increases have made Macs more expensive, but the company isn’t alone in raising prices. Lenovo also announced price rises in June 2026, while other PC manufacturers have warned that soaring memory and storage costs are putting pressure on margins, making higher prices increasingly likely across the industry. As a result, the price gap between Macs and comparable Windows laptops may not be as large as it first appears.





5.
How long will a MacBook last?
The typical lifespan of a MacBook is generally between five and eight years, though this depends heavily on a combination of hardware durability and ongoing software support . While the physical components are built to last, Apple eventually classifies older models as “vintage” or “obsolete,” which limits your ability to get official repairs and parts. Find out more here: How long do MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.





Why you can trust Macworld

Nobody knows Apple better, except probably Apple, but the difference is that we are completely impartial. title: Leak reveals ‘precise updates’ on the next frenzy of Apple launches
content:
Macworld





Apple has launched a succession of groundbreaking products this fall, and the company’s schedule isn’t going to get any quieter next year. A new report claims that no fewer than eight major products will be unveiled in the first half of 2027 alone.
In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg leaker Mark Gurman offers what he describes as “some more precise updates” on “a slew of new products for the iOS 27.4 release cycle early next year.” Apple, he claims, plans to focus on the budget segment of its line-up after a string of more premium releases this fall.
On the all-important iPhone front, we can expect just as many new models (three) as we got in September and October. For the first time, the standard iPhone was decoupled from its Pro siblings this fall, so the iPhone 18 is obviously overdue. Gurman says it will appear in the same February/March timeframe as the iPhone 18e, which was always expected to launch in the spring. The 2nd-gen iPhone Air is coming too, as many will have suspected when a dummy unit with a second camera leaked last week, but Gurman cautions that it is “a little bit behind the lower-end fare” on Apple’s manufacturing schedule and may arrive later.
On this point, Gurman emphasises that Apple is looking to depart from the “small number of very high-profile product launches” strategy it pursued in the past, so we may not get a single flagpole spring event. Rather, Apple intends to split its releases into smaller events and “experiences” as we saw in spring and fall this year. “It all fits into new CEO John Ternus’ desire to launch more products across more periods throughout the year,” he explains.
As for the iPad range, only one truly budget model remains to be launched for the current generation: the 12th-gen iPad, which we can also expect some time in February or March. This is a key launch because it will finally bring Apple Intelligence to the cheapest iPad model. Apple is also working on an OLED iPad Air and an updated iPad Pro for release in the first half of 2027, but as with the iPhone Air 2, these costlier options are likely to lag a little behind the vanilla model.
Finally, the Mac lineup has two new models on the way early next year. The hugely anticipated follow-up to 2026’s popular MacBook Neo should arrive in the late winter or early spring with an A19 Pro chip and more RAM, along with a new M6 MacBook Air. Both are expected to largely be chip bumps.
Assuming Gurman’s sources are accurate, this is a formidable set of launches for the first six months of the year, a time which is normally quieter for Apple. But these products need to be pushed out of the door so the company can turn its attention to higher-profile releases later in 2027, including the iPhone 20 and its first-ever set of smart glasses (which may just sneak into the first half too with a June launch). One way or another, it’s going to be a busy year.

The 13.6-inch Liquid Retina on the M5 MacBook Air display has a native resolution of 2,560×1,664 and 500 nits brightness.
The MacBook Air M5 can support two external displays.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 MacBook Air models supports Thunderbolt 4, which means that they can support a dual monitor set up. If you want to connect USB-A devices, you need either a USB-C to USB-A adapter, like Apple’s $19 / £19 one, or a USB-C hub that has USB-A ports. In the U.K. and Europe Apple has stopped including a Power Adapter in the box, so you will need to buy one separately. See our round-up of the best USB-C hubs and adapters.

How fast is it? The M5 is fast enough for everyday work and occasional creative projects. In our tests the M5 saw consistent gains over the M4 in the previous generation, as you can see in our Mac processor benchmarks. In some benchmarks the M5 even beats the M1 Ultra. If you are upgrading from an old Mac – especially if it is one with an Intel chip – you will see a huge difference.
Any other considerations? The MacBook Air is more than fast enough for everyday use and occasional creative work. Its fanless design keeps it silent, but performance can drop during sustained demanding tasks as it reduces speed to control heat. If you regularly run lengthy video exports, large code builds or other intensive workloads, a MacBook Pro with active cooling is a better choice. Memory and internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase, so choose a configuration that meets your likely longer-term needs. Prioritize enough memory for your apps; you can add storage later with an external SSD. The Air still uses M5, while Apple now offers M6 versions of the standard MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac mini. An M6 MacBook Air could follow in spring 2027. If you need a new laptop now, the M5 Air remains a capable option, particularly at a discount.

What is it? The M6 Mac mini is Apple’s smallest and most affordable desktop Mac. It has the same compact 5×5-inch design introduced with the M4 Mac mini in 2024, but the M6 replaces the M4 chip inside. Unlike an iMac, the Mac mini doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse, so it is particularly attractive if you already own those things. There is also a more powerful Mac mini with an M5 Pro chip, which we discuss separately. Note that while M5 Pro name indicates that the chip is an older generaion, it is still considerably more powerful  than the M6.
What’s new? Apple updated the Mac mini with the M6 chip in August 2026, on-sale from September 22. The design hasn’t changed, but there are some significant improvements inside. The M6 has a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from 10 CPU and GPU cores in the M4, along with Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and Apple’s first Dual 16-core Neural Engine. Maximum unified memory remains 32GB, while memory bandwidth increases from 120GB/s on M4 to 153GB/s with 16GB memory, or 170GB/s with 24GB or 32GB. Apple also says storage is up to twice as fast. Connectivity has been upgraded with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard.
Who’s it for? The M6 Mac mini is a good choice for anyone who wants a powerful desktop Mac but doesn’t need the additional performance of the M5 Pro Mac mini or Mac Studio. It has more than enough power for everyday work, web browsing and office apps, but is also capable of photo and video editing, coding and gaming. Apple is particularly pushing the M6 Mac mini for AI workloads, including running local AI models and AI agents. If your work involves demanding video production, 3D rendering, large AI models or other processor-intensive professional workflows, the M5 Pro version will be a better choice.
How much does the Mac mini cost? The M6 Mac mini starts at $899/£899 with 16GB unified memory and a 256GB SSD. That’s $100/£100 more than the M4 Mac mini cost immediately before it was replaced, and $300/£300 more than the M4 model’s original $599/£599 launch price in October 2024. A 16GB model with 512GB storage costs $1,099/£1,099. There is also an M6 configuration with 24GB memory and 512GB storage for $1,299/£1,299, while additional memory and storage upgrades can be selected when you order.
What are the specifications? 
Apple M6, 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB memory, 256GB SSD, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2 USB-C, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet, $899/£899.
Additional options: 24GB or 32GB unified memory; up to 2TB SSD, and 10Gb Ethernet
The Mac mini does not include a display, keyboard, or mouse, so you’ll have to provide your own, or you can customize your order to include these devices as extra-cost options.
How do I connect stuff? There are two USB-C ports on the front of the Mac mini, supporting USB 3 at up to 10Gb/s, alongside a 3.5mm headphone jack. On the back are three Thunderbolt 4/USB-C ports capable of speeds up to 40Gb/s, an HDMI port and a 2.5Gb Ethernet port. The Ethernet connection can be upgraded to 10Gb when you order. Wireless connectivity has also been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and the Mac mini includes Thread networking support. The M6 model can drive as many as three displays, including two 6K screens and a third 5K display. Unlike some older Mac mini models, there are no USB-A ports, so you’ll need an adapter or hub for older USB accessories.
How fast is it?  In Macwelt’s tests of an M6 Mac mini with 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD, Geekbench 7 single-core performance rose from 3,277 on the M4 mini to 4,055, while multicore rose from 15,693 to 22,695. GPU compute was roughly 70–80 percent higher in its Geekbench 7 and Cinebench 2024 tests. Gaming improved too, although the demanding Steel Nomad test still produced a low frame rate. The M6 is a strong choice for everyday work and moderately demanding creative tasks; sustained GPU-heavy work and larger local AI models are reasons to consider the M5 Pro.
Any other considerations? As with other current Macs, the unified memory and internal SSD can’t be upgraded after purchase, so think carefully about how much memory and storage you’ll need before you order. The 256GB SSD is likely to feel restrictive if you store lots of photos, video or large applications and we’d consider 24GB memory if you want to run more demanding creative or AI workloads. The base 256GB model also uses a single NAND storage package, which could limit SSD speeds compared with the 512GB model’s reported dual-package design, although we don’t yet have benchmarks establishing the difference. Read more about the Mac mini’s storage changes. If you need more memory, Thunderbolt 5, or stronger multicore CPU and GPU performance for demanding workloads, look at the M5 Pro Mac mini instead. Display, keyboard and mouse not included.
Why we recommend the Mac mini M6: Though not as affordable as it once was, the Mac mini is an appealing way to get a powerful Mac if you already own a display, keyboard and mouse. Its combination of a tiny footprint, extensive connectivity and enough performance for everything from everyday work to photo and video editing makes it one of Apple’s most versatile Macs.

What is it? The M5 Pro Mac mini is the more powerful of the two Mac mini models introduced in August 2026. It uses the same compact five-by-five-inch design as the M6 Mac mini (and the predecessor), but substitutes the more powerful M5 Pro chip and Thunderbolt 5 connectivity. Despite the apparently older chip name, M5 Pro is significantly more capable than M6 for demanding professional workloads, with more CPU and GPU cores, greater memory bandwidth, support for up to 64GB of unified memory, and support for three 6K displays.
What’s new? The higher-end Mac mini moved from M4 Pro to M5 Pro in August 2026, on-sale from September 22. It now offers up to an 18-core CPU, 64GB unified memory and 307GB/s memory bandwidth, plus Neural Accelerators in every GPU core. Connectivity improves with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and standard 2.5Gb Ethernet, while genlock over USB-C supports professional video workflows.
Who’s it for? The M5 Pro Mac mini is for developers, video editors, 3D artists, musicians, researchers and other creative or technical professionals who need more processing and graphics power than the standard Mac mini offers, but don’t need to step up to a Mac Studio. It’s particularly well suited to running larger local AI models thanks to its 307GB/s memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory. Apple also highlights app development, video rendering, scientific simulations, 3D design, VFX and game development as suitable workloads. For ordinary office work, web browsing, photo editing and less demanding creative work, the M6 Mac mini should be more than sufficient and costs considerably less.
How much does the Mac mini cost? The M5 Pro Mac mini starts at $1,699/£1,699 with 24GB unified memory and a 512GB SSD. That’s $100/£100 more than the M4 Pro model cost following Apple’s June 2026 price increase, and $300/£300 more than the M4 Pro Mac mini’s original $1,399/£1,399 launch price.
What are the specifications? The standard M5 Pro Mac mini configuration is:
Apple M5 Pro, 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB memory, 512GB SSD, three Thunderbolt 5 ports, 2 USB-C, HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet, $1,699/£1,699
Additional options: M5 Pro with 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU; 48GB or 64GB unified memory; up to 8TB SSD, and 10Gb Ethernet
The Mac mini does not include a display, keyboard, or mouse, so you’ll have to provide your own, or you can customize your order to include these devices as extra-cost options.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 Pro Mac mini has two USB-C/USB 3 ports and a headphone jack on the front. On the back are three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI and Ethernet. Thunderbolt 5 offers transfer speeds up to 120Gbps and can also be used for display, storage, docks and other high-performance peripherals. It can drive up to three 6K displays. Wireless connectivity is Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, while wired networking is now 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, with 10Gb Ethernet available as an option. Apple has also introduced genlock over USB-C, which will be useful in professional video setups where cameras and displays need to be synchronized.
How fast is it?  The M5 Pro Mac mini offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU, with 307GB/s of memory bandwidth. In our review of the M5 Pro Mac mini, Geekbench 7 single-core and multicore scores were 12 percent and 38 percent higher, respectively, than those of the tested M4 Pro mini; GPU compute improved by around 20 percent. In Macwelt’s separate tests, the M5 Pro held a substantial multicore CPU and GPU lead over the M6, although the M6 scored higher in single-core CPU performance. The M5 Pro is therefore better suited to heavily threaded and GPU-intensive work, as well as tasks that need more than the M6’s maximum 32GB of memory.
Any other considerations? Unified memory cannot be upgraded later, and the M5 Pro’s storage chips are now soldered to the logic board, unlike the removable SSD module in the M4 Pro. Choose enough internal storage when ordering, or add capacity later with an external SSD. You’ll also need your own display, keyboard and mouse. Check the price of the exact configuration you need against a Mac Studio: the M5 Pro mini we reviewed, with the full chip, 48GB of memory, a 1TB SSD and 10Gb Ethernet, cost $2,899. Our reviewer compared it with a $2,799 M5 Max Mac Studio with a stronger GPU and more ports, but 36GB rather than 48GB of memory. The M6 mini costs considerably less if you don’t need the M5 Pro’s multicore and GPU performance, memory capacity or Thunderbolt 5.
Why we recommend the Mac mini (M5 Pro): It’s not as affordable as it once was, but the M5 Pro Mac mini packs impressive professional-level performance into an exceptionally small desktop. Compared with the M6 model, it offers more CPU and GPU cores, almost twice the memory bandwidth, up to 64GB unified memory, Thunderbolt 5, and support for three 6K displays. It’s a good choice for developers, video editors, 3D artists and people running larger local AI models who need its particular capabilities, provided the configuration they require still costs less than a suitable Mac Studio. If upgrades push the mini close to Studio pricing, compare memory, GPU performance and ports before ordering.

What is it? The Mac Studio with M5 Max is Apple’s high-performance compact desktop for professional users. It sits between the Mac mini with M5 Pro and the more expensive M5 Ultra version of the Mac Studio. It doesn’t come with a display, keyboard or mouse, but its small desktop design packs in performance and connectivity. The M5 Max version supports up to 128GB of unified memory and five external displays.
What’s new? Apple updated the Mac Studio in August 2026, replacing the M4 Max chip in the model introduced in March 2025 with the M5 Max. The design hasn’t changed, but there are significant upgrades inside. The M5 Max has an 18-core CPU and up to 40-core GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core for much faster AI processing. Memory bandwidth is 460GB/s on the standard model and rises to 614GB/s with the 40-core GPU, storage is up to twice as fast, and the Mac Studio gains Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has also added support for genlock over USB-C and Thunderbolt 5 clustering, which allows multiple Mac Studios to work together on distributed AI workloads.
Who’s it for? The Mac Studio with M5 Max is aimed at creative and technical professionals who need more performance than a Mac mini can provide, but don’t need the extreme power – or price – of the M5 Ultra. Apple specifically highlights musicians, photographers, software developers, engineers and designers working with 3D and motion graphics. It’s also a strong choice for video editing, software development, AI image and video generation, and running large language models locally. If your work involves exceptionally large AI models, complex VFX simulations or huge quantities of 8K video, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio may be more appropriate.
How much does the Mac Studio cost? The M5 Max Mac Studio starts at $2,499/£2,499. That gets you the M5 Max with an 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory and 512GB SSD. The starting price hasn’t changed from the price Apple introduced in June 2026, but it is substantially higher than the previous model’s original launch price: the M4 Max Mac Studio started at $1,999/£2,099 when it arrived in March 2025.
What are the specifications? The entry-level M5 Max Mac Studio offers:
Apple M5 Max, 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 512GB SSD, $2,499/£2,499.
Additional options: M5 Max SoC with an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU; up to 128GB unified memory with the 40-core GPU configuration; up to 8TB SSD storage.
The memory bandwidth of the M5 Max is 460GB/s for the 32-core GPU configuration, or 614GB/s for the 40-core GPU configuration, compared to 546GB/s for the M4 Max model.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 Max Mac Studio has the following ports:
Four Thunderbolt 5 ports on the back supporting speeds of up to 120Gb/s.
Two USB-C ports on the front (these are Thunderbolt on the M5 Ultra model).
SDXC Card slot on the front.
Two USB-A ports.
10Gb ethernet.
HDMI.
3.5 mm headphone jack
Wi-Fi 7.
Bluetooth 6.
The M5 Max supports up to five external displays. The Mac Studio doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse, so you’ll need to provide your own or add Apple’s as extra-cost options.
How fast is it? Our tested M5 Max Mac Studio delivered approximately 23 percent higher multicore performance in Geekbench 7 and 33 percent higher GPU rendering performance in Cinebench 2024 than the tested M4 Max Studio. Storage showed an even bigger improvement: the 4TB SSD achieved approximately 2.7 times the read throughput and 2.2 times the write throughput. However, our video export and encoding tests showed more modest gains, so the benefit will depend on your workload. These results come from a configuration with an 18-core CPU, 40-core GPU, 128GB of unified memory and a 4TB SSD. They should not be treated as measurements of the entry-level model.
Any other considerations? Before choosing the Studio, consider whether a Mac mini would meet your needs for less. In Cinebench 2026, our tested M5 Max Studio scored approximately 75 percent higher in GPU rendering, but only 5 percent higher in multicore CPU rendering than the tested M5 Pro mini. If your work mainly depends on CPU performance and fits within the mini’s memory limits, the smaller Mac may offer better value. The Studio makes a stronger case for demanding GPU workloads and users who need more memory or connectivity. Both desktops require a separate display, keyboard and mouse or trackpad, so factor those into your budget. Choose your configuration carefully: unified memory cannot be upgraded later. The Mac Studio retains removable storage modules, but check compatibility and installation requirements. 
Why we recommend the Mac Studio (M5 Max): The Mac Studio with M5 Max strikes a strong balance between performance and price for professionals who rely on processor- and graphics-intensive apps. Its 18-core CPU, powerful GPU, up to 128GB of unified memory and high memory bandwidth make it well suited to video editing, 3D rendering, software development, music production and AI workloads, especially if you regularly spend time waiting for projects to render, compile or export.
At $2,499/£2,499 it isn’t cheap, and you’ll still need to provide a display and peripherals, but it offers substantially more GPU performance, greater memory capacity and more connectivity than the M5 Pro Mac mini, while costing far less than the $5,499/£5,499 M5 Ultra model. With the Mac Pro discontinued, the Mac Studio is now Apple’s highest-performance desktop and the best fit for many creative professionals, developers, engineers and other power users. What is it? The iMac is Apple’s all-in-one desktop, combining a computer and 24-inch display with a camera, speakers, keyboard and mouse. Its slim enclosure and seven color options make it an attractive choice for a home office, shared family workspace or business reception.
What’s new? Apple announced the M6 iMac on October 27, 2026, replacing the M4 generation and skipping M5. The main changes are additional CPU and GPU cores, improved AI processing, faster storage and upgraded connectivity, including Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and available 2.5Gb Ethernet. The design, colors, display and camera remain unchanged. 
Who’s it for? The iMac suits families, students, home workers and small businesses that want a complete desktop setup with minimal clutter. It should also handle photo editing and other creative work, although demanding professional workloads may justify a Mac mini with M5 Pro or a Mac Studio. Those models also let you choose a larger display.
How much does the iMac cost? The two-port M6 iMac starts at $1,499/£1,499, while the four-port version starts at $1,699/£1,699. Both include 16GB of unified memory and a 256GB SSD. These starting prices match the outgoing M4 models following Apple’s June 2026 price increases.
What are the specifications? There are two main hardware versions, with different processors, connections and upgrade limits:
Two-port iMac: M6 with a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, 16GB memory and a 256GB SSD, from $1,499/£1,499. Configurable with 24GB memory and up to 1TB storage.
Four-port iMac: M6 with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, 16GB memory and a 256GB SSD, from $1,699/£1,699. Configurable with 24GB or 32GB memory and up to 2TB storage.

How fast is it?: Apple claims up to 1.5 times faster performance in productivity tasks such as Excel, twice the graphics performance in selected workloads, and five times faster local AI prompt processing than M4. The iMac’s integrated design is convenient, but a separate computer and monitor offer more flexibility when upgrading.

For buyers who need its additional features, the $1,699/£1,699 four-port model is worth the extra $200/£200: it adds more CPU and GPU cores, two additional ports, a Touch ID keyboard and included Ethernet, plus higher memory and storage limits.
